A.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: What is Cullen sign?
opts: Palatal petechiae
Palatal petechiae are a mucosal bleeding finding in the mouth. Cullen sign is periumbilical ecchymosis.
Yellow sclerae
Yellow sclerae are scleral icterus. Cullen sign is periumbilical ecchymosis.
Flank ecchymosis
Flank ecchymosis is Grey Turner sign. Cullen sign is around the umbilicus.
Periumbilical ecchymosis
Correct. Cullen sign is periumbilical ecchymosis, a sign of internal bleeding. Grey Turner sign is flank ecchymosis.

A.io: Define the physical examination findings of peripheral edema
A.q: What does edema do to the surface anatomy of a limb?
opts: Makes veins and tendons more prominent
Edema obscures them rather than highlighting them.
Produces hair loss over the shins
Loss of hair is a feature of chronic arterial insufficiency.
It obscures veins, tendons and bones
Correct, which is why inspection notes relative size, symmetry and the prominence of those structures — and why one limb is always compared with the other.
Changes skin color to brown
Brown pigmentation is hemosiderin staining, a feature of chronic venous insufficiency.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 87

A.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: Damage to the posterior columns in B12 deficiency impairs which sensations?
opts: Taste and smell
Taste and smell are cranial nerve senses. The posterior columns carry vibration and position sense.
Sight and hearing
Visual changes are possible in B12 deficiency, but they do not come from the posterior columns, which carry vibration and position sense.
Vibration and position
Correct. Posterior column involvement impairs vibration and position sense; corticospinal tract involvement may add spasticity and hyperreflexia.
Pain and temperature
Pain and temperature are not the posterior column modalities named. Vibration and position sense are.

A.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
A.q: Which conditions can produce a pulsation more prominent than the apex beat?
opts: Chronic venous insufficiency
That is a peripheral vascular condition producing skin changes rather than a precordial pulsation.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis produces a low-pitched diastolic rumble rather than a prominent precordial pulsation.
Right ventricular hypertrophy or aortic aneurysm

Correct, with left ventricular hypertrophy and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease also named — so the most prominent pulsation is not always the apex. A dilated pulmonary artery and COPD also do it.
Anxiety and hyperthyroidism
Those produce a hyperkinetic impulse from transiently increased stroke volume rather than displacing the most prominent pulsation.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 19

A.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: A patient reports red or maroon blood passed per rectum. What is this called?
opts: Hematochezia
Correct. Hematochezia is red or maroon blood per rectum. Black, tarry stool is melena, and blood or coffee-ground emesis is hematemesis.
Hematemesis
Hematemesis is blood or coffee-ground emesis, from the mouth. Blood per rectum that is red or maroon is hematochezia.
Epistaxis
Epistaxis is a nosebleed, part of the easy-bleeding questions. Red or maroon blood per rectum is hematochezia.
Melena
Melena is black, tarry stool, not red or maroon blood. Red or maroon blood per rectum is hematochezia.

A.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
A.q: Which condition is a cause of hemoptysis?
opts: Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax brings sudden unilateral pleuritic pain and dyspnea, not coughed-up blood.
Atelectasis
Atelectasis is collapsed lung, the commonest respiratory problem after surgery, and is not a cause of hemoptysis.
Asthma
Asthma brings episodic wheezing, cough and chest tightness; it is not among the causes of hemoptysis.
Bronchiectasis
Correct: the causes are bacterial pneumonias, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pulmonary tuberculosis, lung abscess, lung cancer and pulmonary embolism.

A.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
A.q: What is the more common mechanism of S4?
opts: Sudden opening of a stenotic mitral valve

Abrupt deceleration as a stenotic mitral valve opens produces an opening snap, a high-pitched, very early diastolic sound. S4 is dull and low-pitched, late in diastole. The tell: the snap is heard with the diaphragm right after S2, while S4 needs the bell at the apex just before S1.
Hypertrophy or fibrosis stiffening the ventricle

Correct. The stem asks for the MORE COMMON mechanism of S4: ventricular hypertrophy or fibrosis makes the ventricle stiff, so it resists filling after atrial contraction (decreased compliance). The causes follow from that, namely hypertensive heart disease, aortic stenosis, ischemic and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and delayed conduction between the atria and ventricles.
High filling pressures with abrupt deceleration of inflow

High left ventricular filling pressures with abrupt deceleration of inflow are the mechanism of a pathologic S3, the ventricular gallop, at the end of the rapid filling phase. S4 is the atrial gallop, tied to atrial contraction. The tell: S3 comes early in diastole after S2 (Ken-TUC-ky); S4 comes late, just before S1 (Ten-nes-SEE).
Turbulent flow across an incompetent valve

Turbulent flow across an incompetent valve is regurgitation, which produces a murmur, not a gallop. S4 comes from the atrium contracting into a stiff ventricle. The tell: regurgitation is a 'swoosh' of backward flow, while S4 is a dull, low-pitched sound just before S1 (Ten-nes-SEE).
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 42

A.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: What pulse oximetry reading is typical in an anemic patient with dyspnea and no lung disease?
opts: Unreadable because of pallor
Pallor does not stop the reading; oximetry is normal despite reduced oxygen content.
Low during exertion
Exertional dyspnea is common, but oximetry stays normal in anemia despite reduced oxygen content.
Low, matching the fall in hemoglobin
Oximetry does not fall with the hemoglobin. It stays normal although oxygen content is reduced.
Normal, despite reduced oxygen content
Correct. Pulse oximetry is normal despite reduced oxygen content: lower hemoglobin lowers the oxygen-carrying capacity, not the saturation of the hemoglobin present.

A.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
A.q: Which component of S2 is usually louder, and why?
opts: Whichever closes second
Loudness is attributed to the pressure in the aorta rather than to the order of closure.
Pulmonic, because the valve is closer to the chest wall
The aortic component is the louder one, and the reason given is aortic pressure rather than proximity.
Aortic, reflecting the high pressure in the aorta
Correct. A2 and P2 are the two components, and the pressure difference between the two circuits is what makes the aortic one dominate.
They are always equal in intensity
The aortic component is usually the louder of the two, reflecting the high pressure in the aorta.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 14

A.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
A.q: A patient says they coughed up blood. What should be done before the term hemoptysis is used in the chart?
opts: Confirm it has happened more than once
Repeat episodes are not required; ask when it first started to judge acute against chronic, and confirm where the blood came from.
Confirm the blood was bright red
Color helps (stomach blood is darker), but blood from the nasopharynx can be aspirated and coughed out, so the source must be confirmed.
Confirm the source of the bleeding
Correct: hemoptysis is blood from the LOWER respiratory tract; blood may come from the nose, mouth, pharynx or gastrointestinal tract, so confirm the source first.
Confirm the volume exceeds 600 mL
More than 600 mL in 24 hours defines MASSIVE hemoptysis; any amount from the lower respiratory tract is still hemoptysis.

A.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
A.q: Describe the murmur of aortic stenosis.
opts: Midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, harsh
Correct, in the aortic area, radiating often to the carotids, down the left sternal border and even to the apex. A thrill implies grade 4 or above. The pitch is medium.
Mid to late diastolic, low-pitched rumble
Aortic stenosis is not diastolic: its murmur is midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, medium-pitched and harsh.
Early diastolic, decrescendo, high frequency
Aortic stenosis is a systolic murmur, not early diastolic: midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo and harsh.
Pansystolic, plateau, medium and blowing
Aortic stenosis is not pansystolic or blowing: it is midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, medium-pitched and harsh.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 67

A.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
A.q: Where is a right-sided S4 heard, and how does it behave with respiration?
opts: At the apex, louder with expiration
The apex is where the left-sided S4 is heard with the bell in left lateral decubitus.
In the aortic area, unchanged by respiration
The aortic area is a site for ejection sounds and the murmur of aortic stenosis.
Over the carotids, louder with expiration
The carotids carry the radiation of aortic stenosis rather than a gallop.
Lower left sternal border, louder with inspiration
Correct, and it is associated with pulmonary hypertension and pulmonic stenosis. The left-sided S4 is heard at the apex.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 42

A.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
A.q: Which history is associated with a mediastinal crunch?
opts: An autoimmune disease
Autoimmune disease is relevant history for interstitial lung disease, whose sound is fine crackles.
A long period of immobility
Immobility is relevant history for pulmonary embolism, which gives sudden dyspnea, not a crunch in time with the heart.
Rapid ascent from scuba diving
Correct: the crunch is associated with tracheobronchial injury, blunt trauma, pulmonary edema, recreational drugs, childbirth and rapid ascent from scuba diving.
Exposure to allergens and cold air
Allergens and cold air are asthma triggers; asthma gives wheezes, not precordial crackles with each heartbeat.

A.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
A.q: What does a sustained ventricular impulse indicate?
opts: Ventricular dilation from increased preload
That produces a diffuse impulse, from chronic volume overload.
Hypertrophy from chronic pressure load
Correct — increased afterload. Aortic stenosis and hypertension are the examples, and the duration is sustained rather than under two thirds of systole. That is increased afterload.
Inflammation of the pericardial sac
That produces a pericardial friction rub rather than a change in the impulse.
Transiently increased stroke volume
That produces a hyperkinetic impulse, which does not necessarily indicate heart disease.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 22

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
A.q: What is the main limitation of chest percussion?
opts: It cannot detect deep-seated lesions
Correct: percussion shows whether underlying tissue is air-filled, fluid-filled or consolidated, but it cannot help with deep-seated lesions.
It cannot tell air from fluid
Telling air-filled from fluid-filled or consolidated tissue is exactly what percussion does; its limit is deep-seated lesions.
It cannot detect a pleural effusion
A pleural effusion is detected as dullness over the fluid, with a high level of diaphragmatic excursion.
It cannot detect a pneumothorax
A large pneumothorax is detected as unilateral hyperresonance or a tympanic note on the affected side.

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
A.q: Which breathing pattern is defined by prolonged expiration from narrowed airways and increased airflow resistance?
opts: Bradypnea
Bradypnea is slow breathing, with or without increased tidal volume, rather than prolonged expiration.
Tachypnea
Tachypnea is rapid, shallow breathing; it is defined by rate and depth, not by a prolonged expiration.
Sighing respiration
Sighing respiration is frequent sighs interrupting breathing; occasional sighs are normal and do not prolong expiration.
Obstructive breathing
Correct: obstructive breathing is prolonged expiration due to narrowed airways and increased airflow resistance, which is why the survey notes whether expiration lasts longer than usual.

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
A.q: Which breathing pattern is defined as rapid, shallow breathing?
opts: Tachypnea
Correct: tachypnea is rapid, shallow breathing; rapid DEEP breathing is the separate pattern of hyperpnea or hyperventilation.
Cheyne-Stokes breathing
Cheyne-Stokes breathing is deep breathing alternating with apnea, not a steady rapid, shallow pattern.
Hyperpnea
Hyperpnea is rapid DEEP breathing that responds to metabolic demand, not rapid shallow breathing.
Bradypnea
Bradypnea is the opposite: slow breathing, with or without increased tidal volume.

A.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: In an anemic patient, which travel detail should be asked about?
opts: Jet lag and sleep loss
Fatigue from jet lag is not the concern. Ask about destination, timing, febrile illness and infectious exposures.
Airline and seat class
Travel logistics do not matter. The questions are destination, timing, febrile illness and infectious exposures.
Febrile illness or infections
Correct. The travel history asks destination, timing, febrile illness and infectious exposures; malaria, for example, is an extrinsic cause of hemolysis.
Altitude of the destination
Altitude is not on the travel history. It asks destination, timing, febrile illness and infectious exposures.

A.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
A.q: Which question assesses the functional severity of dyspnea?
opts: Did it start suddenly or gradually?
Sudden or gradual is the ONSET of the symptom, which characterizes dyspnea rather than measuring its functional severity.
What makes it better or worse?
Triggers and relievers characterize dyspnea; functional severity asks about stairs, distance and daily tasks.
How many flights of stairs can you climb?
Correct: functional severity is graded by walking distance, flights of stairs without stopping, everyday tasks and change from baseline.
Is it worse when you lie flat?
Body position is part of characterizing the symptom; severity is measured by what the patient can still do.

A.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: Which part of the eye is inspected for the pallor of anemia?
opts: The retina
The retina is not where pallor is looked for. Pull the lower lid down and look at the palpebral conjunctiva.
The iris
Iris color says nothing about anemia. Pallor is sought in the palpebral conjunctiva.
The conjunctiva
Correct. Pallor is looked for in the palpebral conjunctiva (pull the lower lid down), with the oral mucosa; the sclera is inspected separately for icterus.
The sclera
The sclera is inspected for icterus (yellowing), not pallor. Pallor is judged on the palpebral conjunctiva.

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
A.q: Bronchial breath sounds are heard over the lung bases, where vesicular sounds are expected. What does this suggest?
opts: A pneumothorax
A pneumothorax gives decreased or absent breath sounds with hyperresonance, not bronchial sounds at the bases.
A normal variant at the bases
Bronchial sounds are normal only over the manubrium; at the bases they are abnormal and suggest consolidation.
Hyperinflated lung
Hyperinflated lung, as in obstructive disease, gives decreased or distant breath sounds, not bronchial sounds.
Consolidated or fluid-filled lung
Correct: bronchovesicular or bronchial sounds in unexpected places mean air-filled lung has been replaced by fluid-filled or consolidated tissue, as in lobar pneumonia.

A.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
A.q: Can the neurologic findings of B12 deficiency occur without anemia?
opts: Yes, even without anemia
Correct. Neurologic findings of B12 deficiency can occur without anemia or macrocytosis, so a normal blood count does not rule out the deficiency in a patient with these findings.
With severe anemia, not mild
Severity is not required; findings can occur with no anemia at all.
No, anemia comes first
Neurologic findings can appear without anemia or macrocytosis.
When macrocytosis is present
They can occur without macrocytosis as well as without anemia.

A.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
A.q: What are varicosities?
opts: Ulceration around the medial malleolus

Ulceration over the medial and lateral malleolus is the typical ulcer of chronic venous insufficiency, with small, painful granulation tissue and irregular borders, not a varicosity. Varicosities are dilated veins. The tell: an ulcer is a break in the skin at the ankle, while a varicosity is a widened vein along the leg.
Brown discoloration from hemosiderin

Brown discoloration from hemosiderin staining is a pigment change of chronic venous insufficiency, a consequence of venous disease rather than the dilated veins themselves. Varicosities are the veins, mildly to severely dilated. The tell: hemosiderin is a color in the skin, while a varicosity is a shape, a widened vein.
Thickened arterial walls with reduced elasticity

Varicosities are a disorder of veins, not arteries, so thickened arterial walls cannot define them. Arterial disease shows up on exam as absent or decreased pulses, which may suggest atherosclerosis or systemic embolism. The tell: varicosities are dilated veins you look for on inspection, while arterial disease is found by palpating the pulses.
Mild to severe dilatation of veins

Correct. Varicosities are mild to severe dilatation of the veins, mainly in the lower extremities, which is the definition the stem asks for. They are one of the skin changes to look for, and venous varicosities are among the associated findings of chronic venous insufficiency, alongside edema, purpura, stasis dermatitis and cyanosis of the foot when dependent.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 95

A.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
A.q: What produces the second heart sound?
opts: Turbulent flow across a narrowed valve

Turbulent flow across a narrowed valve produces a murmur, a 'swoosh' such as aortic stenosis, rather than a discrete heart sound. S2 is a brief sound made by two valves closing as the ventricles relax. The tell: a murmur lasts through part of systole or diastole, while S2 is the single 'dub' that marks the start of diastole.
Closure of the pulmonic and aortic valves

Correct. S2 comes at the start of diastole: as the ventricles start to relax, the pulmonic and aortic valves close, and that closure is the second heart sound. It has two parts, aortic (A2), usually louder because of the high pressure in the aorta, and pulmonic (P2), normally fused on expiration and audibly split on inspiration.
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves

Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves produces S1, at the start of systole, when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure. S2 comes at the start of diastole from the other pair of valves. The tell: the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) close for S1, the 'lub'; the aortic and pulmonic valves close for S2, the 'dub'.
Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle

Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle produces S4, the atrial gallop, an extra sound late in diastole just before S1. S2 is a normal heart sound made by valves closing, not by the atrium contracting. The tell: S4 needs reduced compliance from hypertrophy or fibrosis, while S2 is one of the two normal heart sounds, the 'dub'.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 14

A.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
A.q: Where and how is S1 best heard, and what is its relation to the carotid pulse?
opts: Diaphragm at the apex, before the carotid pulse
Correct, and splitting is usually not present. The carotid relationship is what makes palpating the carotid a reliable way to time the cycle.
With the diaphragm at the base, preceding the carotid pulse
S1 is best heard at the apex rather than the base; the base is where S2 is best appreciated.
With the bell at the base, following the carotid pulse
S2 is best heard with the diaphragm at the base and FOLLOWS the carotid pulse, the reverse of S1.
With the bell at the apex, following the carotid pulse
S1 is best heard with the diaphragm and it precedes the carotid pulse.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 34

A.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: Which question about bleeding belongs in the history of an anemic patient?
opts: The patient's blood type
Blood type does not identify a bleeding source. The history asks about bruising, nosebleeds, gum bleeding and prolonged procedural bleeding.
Whether the patient has ever donated blood
Blood donation is not on the bleeding history. It asks about easy bruising, nosebleeds, gum bleeding and prolonged bleeding after procedures.
Whether bleeding stops with ice
No such question is part of the history. It covers bruising, nosebleeds, gum bleeding, prolonged procedural bleeding and each source's onset, frequency, amount and duration.
Gum bleeding or nosebleeds
Correct. The bleeding history asks about easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding and prolonged procedural bleeding, then the gastrointestinal, urinary and uterine sources.

A.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: When is a digital rectal examination done in the hematologic examination?
opts: After a positive stool test
It is not limited to that; it is performed when clinically indicated.
When clinically indicated

Correct. A digital rectal examination is performed when clinically indicated, as part of the gastrointestinal examination, which also checks for tenderness, masses, hepatomegaly, ascites and splenomegaly.
It is replaced by stool tests
Stool tests do not replace it, and a negative one does not exclude bleeding. It is done when clinically indicated.
In each patient, whatever the history
It is not routine for everyone; it is done when clinically indicated.

A.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
A.q: What is the apical impulse?
opts: The pulsation of the aortic arch at the sternal notch
That is a separate finding; the apical impulse comes from the left ventricular apex.
The brief impulse of the left ventricular apex
Correct, occurring during contraction and identified on palpation of the precordium as the point of maximal impulse. It strikes the chest wall during contraction.
The impulse of the right ventricle at the lower sternal border
The right ventricular impulse is felt at the 3rd to 5th left intercostal spaces rather than at the apex.
The palpable vibration of a loud murmur
That is a thrill, assessed with the balls of the hand against the chest wall.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 19

A.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
A.q: What are the findings of chronic venous insufficiency?
opts: Mild or no pain, normal temperature, pitting edema

Correct. Chronic venous insufficiency brings a normal skin temperature and pitting edema, and the limb is listed with no pain; the only pain named is the small, painful granulation tissue inside a venous ulcer, which is why 'mild or no pain' fits. The rest of the picture: brownish hemosiderin staining, thickened skin, normal pulses, and gangrene that is rare.
Painful ulceration with thin shiny skin and hair loss

Painful ulceration with thin, shiny skin and hair loss describes chronic ARTERIAL insufficiency, where ulcers are painful unless neuropathy is present. Venous ulcers sit around the ankles, with thickened skin, hemosiderin staining and pitting edema. The tell: thin, shiny, hairless skin is arterial; thick, pigmented skin with edema is venous.
Cool skin with decreased pulses and no edema

Cool skin, decreased pulses and no edema are the findings of chronic ARTERIAL insufficiency. Venous insufficiency is the reverse on all three: normal temperature, normal pulses and pitting edema. The tell: edema with normal pulses points to the veins, while cool skin with weak pulses and no swelling points to the arteries.
Foot pallor on elevation with dusky rubor

Foot pallor on elevation and dusky rubor are listed under chronic arterial insufficiency, with cool skin and decreased pulses. Venous insufficiency colors the skin differently: cyanotic or brownish hemosiderin staining and cyanosis of the foot when dependent. The tell: brown pigment means venous; pallor on elevation means arterial.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 93

A.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: A patient admits to craving and chewing ice. Which deficiency does this suggest?
opts: Folate deficiency
Folate deficiency shares glossitis and angular cheilitis with iron and B12, but pica is the iron clue specifically.
B12 deficiency
B12 deficiency shows as paresthesias, impaired balance and reduced vibration or position sense, not pica. Ice chewing points to iron deficiency.
Lead poisoning
Lead exposure is asked about as an occupational or renovation history, not through ice cravings. Pica for ice points to iron deficiency.
Iron deficiency
Correct. Pica, particularly craving or chewing ice, is an iron deficiency clue, listed with brittle or spoon-shaped nails and hair shedding.

A.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: An anemic patient has increased respiratory effort. What else should be considered?
opts: Anemia alone explains the effort
Anemia causes dyspnea and tachypnea, but coexisting pulmonary disease or heart failure must be considered.
Iron deficiency from the effort
Effort does not cause iron deficiency. Consider coexisting pulmonary disease or heart failure.
A falsely low pulse oximetry reading
Oximetry is typically normal in anemia. Increased effort raises coexisting pulmonary disease or heart failure.
Lung disease or heart failure
Correct. Respiratory effort is assessed for coexisting pulmonary disease or heart failure, which add to the dyspnea and tachypnea of significant anemia.

A.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
A.q: In which position is the mediastinal crunch (Hamman sign) best heard?
opts: Sitting, arms folded
Sitting with arms folded is the position for the posterior lung examination, not for hearing the crunch.
Left lateral decubitus
Correct: the mediastinal crunch, precordial crackles in time with the heartbeat, is best heard with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.
Sitting, leaning forward
Sitting forward is what relieves pericarditis pain; the mediastinal crunch is best heard in the left lateral decubitus position.
Supine
Supine is used for the anterior chest examination; the crunch is best heard in the left lateral decubitus position.

A.io: Review the classic areas of auscultation to assess cardiac sounds
A.q: Which lighting is specified for the cardiovascular examination?
opts: Tangential lighting
Correct, because it casts shadows that reveal the contours of the chest wall — a pulsation visible in raking light can be invisible under direct light. It matters most during inspection.
Dim lighting to reduce patient anxiety
Enough lighting and exposure is required; tangential lighting is the specific instruction.
Colored light to highlight cyanosis
No colored light is described; tangential lighting is what is specified.
Bright overhead lighting
Direct overhead light flattens the contours that inspection is trying to detect.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 26

A.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
A.q: Pain on deep inspiration comes from irritation of which layer?
opts: Bronchial lining
The bronchi carry air to the alveoli; pain with deep inspiration comes from irritation of the parietal pleura.
Parietal pleura
Correct: the parietal pleura is highly innervated by intercostal and phrenic nerves, so irritating it produces pleuritic pain with deep inspiration.
Visceral pleura
The visceral pleura covers the lung surface and lacks sensory nerves, so irritation of it is not the source of pleuritic pain.
Alveolar walls
The alveoli are the site of gas exchange; pleuritic pain comes from the parietal pleura with its intercostal and phrenic nerve supply.

A.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
A.q: Which feature suggests that blood brought up by a patient came from the stomach rather than the respiratory tract?
opts: Darker blood mixed with food particles
Correct: blood from the stomach is darker than respiratory blood and comes with food particles, and vomited blood is likely gastrointestinal.
Blood following a nosebleed
Nasopharyngeal blood can be aspirated and then coughed out; it is not darker or mixed with food the way gastric blood is.
Blood streaks after throat clearing
Blood streaks can come from the nose, mouth or pharynx; darker blood with food particles is what points to the stomach.
Bright red blood after a coughing fit
Blood coughed up from the chest points to the lower respiratory tract; stomach blood is darker and mixed with food.

A.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
A.q: Which maneuvers affect the murmur of aortic stenosis?
opts: Unchanged by any maneuver
Squatting and leg raise both increase it; Valsalva and standing soften it.
Louder with Valsalva and on standing
Those maneuvers reduce preload, which makes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy louder and aortic stenosis softer.
Better sitting forward; louder on squatting
Correct, because both squatting and leg raise increase venous return and preload, sending more blood past the narrowed valve. Leg raise does the same.
Louder with isometric handgrip only
Handgrip raises left-sided afterload and increases mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal defect, aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis; the preload maneuvers are what change aortic stenosis.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 67

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
A.q: Which breath sound is soft and relatively low-pitched, with inspiration lasting longer than expiration, and is heard over most of both lungs?
opts: Bronchial
Bronchial sounds have EXPIRATION longer than inspiration and are loud and relatively high-pitched, over the manubrium.
Tracheal
Tracheal sounds are very loud and relatively high-pitched, with equal phases, over the trachea in the neck.
Vesicular
Correct: vesicular sounds have inspiration longer than expiration, a soft, relatively low-pitched expiratory sound, and are heard over most of both lungs.
Bronchovesicular
Bronchovesicular sounds have inspiration and expiration about EQUAL, intermediate in intensity and pitch, in the 1st and 2nd interspaces and between the scapulae.

A.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
A.q: Slowly progressive exertional dyspnea, scant sputum and later cough in a patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency suggest which diagnosis?
opts: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Correct: this disease is slowly progressive exertional dyspnea with cough developing later, wheezing and scant sputum, with smoking, inhalational exposures or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
Pneumonia
Pneumonia is ACUTE, with fever, chills and sputum, not slowly progressive exertional dyspnea.
Left-sided heart failure
Heart failure is worse lying flat, with orthopnea, edema and weight gain, in cardiac disease or hypertension.
Interstitial lung disease
Interstitial lung disease is tied to autoimmune disease, medications and occupational exposures, not to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

A.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: Besides location and size, which features of an enlarged lymph node should be recorded?
opts: Tenderness, consistency and mobility
Correct. An enlarged node is described by location, size, tenderness, consistency and mobility, the five features to record for any enlarged node.
Blanching, distribution and palpability
Distribution and palpability describe petechiae and purpura, which are nonblanching. Nodes are described by tenderness, consistency and mobility.
Pulsation, warmth and itch
None of these is on the node checklist. After location and size come tenderness, consistency and mobility.
Color, temperature and odor
These are not lymph node descriptors. After location and size, record tenderness, consistency and mobility.

A.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: What does the roof of this patient's mouth show?
opts: Oral mucosal pallor
Pallor would make the mucosa pale. These are red pinpoint hemorrhages: palatal petechiae.
Angular cheilitis
Angular cheilitis is fissuring at the mouth corners. These are pinpoint red dots on the palate.
Glossitis
Glossitis is a smooth, sore, beefy-red tongue. The finding here is pinpoint red dots on the palate.
Palatal petechiae
Correct. Clustered pinpoint red spots on the palate are palatal petechiae, a form of mucosal bleeding, which raises concern when seen with skin petechiae.
A.alt: An open mouth showing the roof of the mouth, with a cluster of small red dots on the soft palate.

A.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
A.q: Where is the needle inserted for a thoracentesis?
opts: Anteriorly, in the 2nd intercostal space
The 2nd intercostal space anteriorly is for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax, not for draining fluid.
Laterally, between the 4th and 5th ribs
The space between the 4th and 5th ribs, in the triangle of safety, is the chest tube site rather than the thoracentesis site.
Posteriorly, just above the 8th rib
Correct: thoracentesis is done at T7-T8, the 7th intercostal space, with the needle immediately superior to the 8th rib, to drain a pleural effusion.
Posteriorly, just below the 8th rib
Entry just BELOW a rib meets the neurovascular structures that run along its inferior margin; the needle goes just above the 8th rib.

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
A.q: How is the carotid examined?
opts: Palpate first, then auscultate
Auscultation comes before palpation, so that the vessel is not disturbed before listening.
Palpate both sides simultaneously to compare
The carotids are palpated ONE AT A TIME, unlike the radial and femoral pulses compared for lag.
Auscultate while the patient breathes normally
The patient is asked to hold their breath, so breath sounds do not obscure a bruit.
Auscultate first, then palpate one side at a time
Correct, with the patient holding their breath, lateral to the trachea. Palpating both at once risks compromising cerebral flow.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 97

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
A.q: How is the ankle brachial index calculated?
opts: Brachial systolic over the higher ankle pressure
The ratio runs the other way, with the ankle pressure on top.
Average of both ankle pressures over the average brachial
The higher single ankle pressure is used rather than an average.
Higher ankle pressure over brachial systolic
Correct, calculated for each leg and recorded to two decimal places. The normal range is 0.90 to 1.40.
Lower of the two ankle pressures over the brachial systolic
The HIGHER of the two ankle artery pressures is used as the numerator rather than the lower.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 110

A.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: Which lymph node groups are examined routinely in the hematologic examination?
opts: Inguinal and femoral
The inguinal region is examined when indicated, not routinely, and femoral nodes are not named. Cervical and supraclavicular are the routine groups.
Mesenteric
Mesenteric nodes cannot be examined at the bedside. Cervical and supraclavicular nodes are.
Cervical and supraclavicular
Correct. The cervical and supraclavicular nodes are examined, and the axillary and inguinal regions when indicated.
Popliteal and epitrochlear
These are not on the list. Cervical and supraclavicular nodes are examined, axillary and inguinal when indicated.

A.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
A.q: What is normal capillary refill time?
opts: Two to three seconds
Correct, tested by pressing on the fingernail and noting how long the nail bed takes to become pink again.
Under one second
The normal window is two to three seconds, so under one second would be unusually brisk.
It varies too much to have a normal value
A normal of two to three seconds is specified, so the measure is not too variable to use.
Five to six seconds
That would be prolonged against the two to three second normal.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 85

A.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
A.q: What produces a murmur?
opts: Abrupt deceleration of a stenotic valve opening

Abrupt deceleration as a stenotic mitral valve opens produces an opening snap, a high-pitched, very early diastolic sound. It is a brief snap, not the sustained sound of turbulent flow. The tell: an opening snap is one sharp sound right after S2, while a murmur is a 'swoosh' that lasts through part of the cycle.
Closure of the atrioventricular valves

Closure of the mitral and tricuspid (atrioventricular) valves produces S1, the 'lub', a brief normal heart sound at the start of systole. A murmur is a longer sound of turbulent blood flow, not a valve closing. The tell: S1 is a discrete normal sound, while a murmur is a 'swoosh' heard across part of the cycle.
Inflammation of the pericardial sac

Inflammation of the pericardial sac is pericarditis, which produces a pericardial friction rub, a scratchy, scraping noise through both systole and diastole. A murmur needs turbulent blood flow, not inflamed pericardium. The tell: the rub is scratchy and comes from the sac around the heart, while a murmur is a 'swoosh' of blood over a valve.
Turbulent blood flow over a valve

Correct. A murmur is the sound made by turbulent blood flow over a heart valve, and it sounds like a 'swoosh'. The turbulence has five named sources: flow across a partially obstructed valve, increased flow through a normal valve of a small child, ejection into a dilated chamber, regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve, and abnormal shunting into a lower pressure chamber.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

A.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
A.q: Which history raises suspicion for pulmonary embolism in a patient with sudden dyspnea?
opts: Cold air and exercise as triggers
Cold air, exercise and allergens are asthma triggers; asthma is episodic rather than sudden and unexplained.
Estrogen use and recent immobility
Correct: the relevant history for pulmonary embolism is prior venous thromboembolism, surgery, immobility, cancer, estrogen and pregnancy or the postpartum period.
Autoimmune disease on new medication
Autoimmune disease and medications are the history for interstitial lung disease, which is gradually progressive.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is relevant history for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which is slowly progressive.

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
A.q: What does an ankle brachial index above 1.40 suggest?
opts: A normal result
Normal runs from 0.90 to 1.40; above that suggests calcification.
Mild peripheral arterial disease
Values below 0.90 suggest peripheral arterial disease, at the opposite end of the scale.
A non-compressible calcified vessel
Correct, and it is the counter-intuitive one — a high value reflects a stiff artery rather than good perfusion.
Severe peripheral arterial disease
That is suggested by a value below 0.50.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 113

A.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
A.q: Which rib does the right horizontal fissure follow?
opts: 6th rib
The 6th rib anteriorly is where the oblique fissures end, not the line of the horizontal fissure, which follows the 4th rib.
2nd rib
The 2nd rib is not where the horizontal fissure runs; the horizontal fissure follows the 4th rib.
8th rib
The 8th rib is where the inferior lung border crosses the midaxillary line; the horizontal fissure follows the 4th rib.
4th rib
Correct: the right horizontal fissure follows the 4th rib and meets the oblique fissure near the 5th rib at the midaxillary line.

A.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
A.q: What is the immediate response to an anemic patient with active major bleeding and hypotension?
opts: Immediate escalation and resuscitation
Correct. Active major bleeding with hypotension calls for immediate escalation: stabilization, bleeding control and resuscitation, with oxygen and transfusion according to the situation.
A complete dietary and travel history first
The detailed history waits; immediate escalation for stabilization and bleeding control comes first.
Repeat hemoglobin in a week
Waiting is unsafe; instability may precede the hemoglobin fall. Escalate immediately.
Outpatient stool blood testing
Stool testing is not the immediate step: active major bleeding with hypotension needs immediate escalation.

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
A.q: Which breath sound is loud and relatively high-pitched, with expiration lasting longer than inspiration, and is normally heard over the manubrium?
opts: Bronchial
Correct: bronchial sounds have expiration longer than inspiration, loud and relatively high-pitched, over the manubrium and larger proximal airways.
Tracheal
Tracheal sounds are very loud with phases about EQUAL, heard over the trachea in the neck rather than the manubrium.
Vesicular
Vesicular sounds are the reverse: INSPIRATION longer than expiration, soft and relatively low-pitched, over most of both lungs.
Bronchovesicular
Bronchovesicular sounds have equal phases and intermediate intensity, in the 1st and 2nd interspaces and between the scapulae.

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
A.q: Before auscultating the lungs, what should the patient be asked to do?
opts: Hold the breath
Breath holding is the test that separates a pleural rub (it disappears) from a pericardial rub, not a step before routine auscultation.
Cough once or twice
Correct: a cough or two clears mild atelectasis or airway mucus that can produce extra sounds; the patient should also be de-robed.
Breathe as shallowly as possible
Shallow breathing does not help; coughing once or twice first clears mucus or mild atelectasis that would add sounds.
Say ninety-nine
Saying a phrase is not a preparation step; the patient is asked to cough once or twice before auscultation.

A.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
A.q: Which of these is a named cause of a murmur?
opts: Inflammation of the pericardium

Inflammation of the pericardial sac (pericarditis) produces a pericardial friction rub, a scratchy, scraping noise, not a murmur. A murmur needs turbulent blood flow over a heart valve or into a chamber. The tell: the rub is heard through both systole and diastole, while every named murmur cause involves blood flow.
Ejection into a dilated chamber

Correct. Ejection into a dilated chamber is one of the five named causes of a murmur, the sound of turbulent blood flow that sounds like a 'swoosh'. The other four are flow across a partially obstructed valve, increased flow through a normal valve in a small child, regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve, and abnormal shunting into a lower pressure chamber.
High left ventricular filling pressure

High left ventricular filling pressure, with abrupt deceleration of inflow, produces a pathologic S3, the ventricular gallop of adults over 40. It is an extra heart sound early in diastole, not a murmur. The tell: the named murmur causes are all about flow through a valve, into a chamber or through a shunt, not how the ventricle fills.
Reduced ventricular compliance

Reduced ventricular compliance, from hypertrophy or fibrosis, produces S4, the atrial gallop, as the atrium contracts against a stiff ventricle. It is an extra heart sound rather than a murmur, so it is not one of the murmur causes. The tell: a gallop is a dull, low-pitched sound just before S1, while a murmur is a 'swoosh' of turbulent flow.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 46

A.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
A.q: At which anterior landmark is a needle inserted to decompress a tension pneumothorax?
opts: 10th intercostal space
The lungs end near the 8th rib at the midaxillary line and T10 posteriorly; the decompression needle goes in at the 2nd space.
7th intercostal space
The 7th intercostal space is the posterior thoracentesis site, immediately above the 8th rib, not the decompression site.
4th intercostal space
The space between the 4th and 5th ribs is the chest tube site; needle decompression is higher, at the 2nd intercostal space.
2nd intercostal space
Correct: the 2nd intercostal space anteriorly is the needle decompression site; the space between the 4th and 5th ribs is kept for chest tubes.

A.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
A.q: A patient with an autoimmune condition has gradually progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough, fatigue and weakness. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is sudden, with abrupt unilateral pleuritic pain, not gradually progressive.
Interstitial lung disease
Correct: gradually progressive exertional dyspnea with dry cough, fatigue and weakness, in autoimmune disease or after medication or occupational exposure, is interstitial lung disease.
Chronic bronchitis
Chronic bronchitis starts with a chronic PRODUCTIVE cough and sputum; this cough is dry.
Asthma
Asthma is episodic with symptom-free intervals and wheezing, not steadily progressive with a dry cough.

A.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
A.q: A patient with suspected internal bleeding has no Cullen or Grey Turner sign. What does this mean?
opts: Significant bleeding is excluded
These signs are uncommon and possibly delayed; absent signs do not exclude bleeding.
Significant bleeding is still possible
Correct. Both signs are uncommon and may appear late, so their absence does not exclude significant bleeding.
Pancreatitis is excluded
Absence rules nothing out: the signs are uncommon and may be delayed.
The bleeding must be menstrual
Their absence does not locate the bleeding; significant internal bleeding is still possible.

A.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
A.q: An abnormally HIGH level of dullness when measuring diaphragmatic excursion suggests which?
opts: Pleural rub at the bases
A pleural rub is an adventitious sound heard on auscultation, not a percussion level.
Effusion or a raised hemidiaphragm
Correct: an abnormally high level suggests a pleural effusion, or an elevated hemidiaphragm from atelectasis or phrenic nerve injury.
Hyperinflation from asthma
Hyperinflated lungs give generalized hyperresonance; a high level of dullness points to fluid or a raised hemidiaphragm.
A large pneumothorax
A pneumothorax gives hyperresonance or a tympanic note, not a high level of dullness at the base.

A.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
A.q: In an anemia or bleeding emergency, how are oxygen and transfusion given?
opts: According to the clinical situation
Correct. Oxygen and transfusion are given according to the clinical situation, alongside immediate escalation: stabilization, bleeding control and resuscitation.
After the history is complete
The emergency calls for immediate escalation, not a finished history first. Oxygen and transfusion are given according to the clinical situation.
To every anemic patient at arrival
They are not given to everyone; oxygen and transfusion follow the clinical situation, after vital signs, mental status, perfusion and ongoing loss are assessed.
Once the hemoglobin has fallen
Waiting for the hemoglobin is unsafe, since instability can precede its fall. Oxygen and transfusion follow the clinical situation.

A.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
A.q: A grating, creaking sound over the lower lateral chest is heard in both phases of breathing and disappears when the patient holds their breath. Which sound is it?
opts: Pericardial friction rub
A pericardial friction rub follows the heart, so it does NOT disappear when the breath is held; that is the distinguishing test.
Pleural rub
Correct: a pleural rub is discontinuous, low-frequency and grating, usually biphasic, and disappears with a breath hold, which separates it from a pericardial friction rub.
Mediastinal crunch
The mediastinal crunch is crackles synchronized with the heartbeat, not with respiration, so it would persist during a breath hold.
Coarse crackles
Coarse crackles are popping sounds from secretions or fluid that do not depend on the pleura and are not described as grating.

A.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
A.q: A patient coughs up large amounts of foul-smelling sputum every day. Which conditions does this suggest?
opts: Bacterial pneumonia or bronchitis
Bacterial pneumonia is the purulent pattern, yellow or green; copious and foul-smelling points elsewhere.
Cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis
Correct: COPIOUS foul-smelling sputum is the pattern for cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis; foul smell alone suggests an anaerobic lung abscess.
Viral infection or postnasal drip
Viral infection and postnasal drip give mucoid sputum: translucent, white or gray, and not foul-smelling.
Asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Asthma brings wheezing, cough and chest tightness, and the obstructive disease scant sputum, not a daily copious foul load.

B.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Which bleeding history in a 62-year-old woman must be asked about specifically?
opts: Cycle length in her twenties
Past cycle length does not identify a present source. Ask about postmenopausal and intermenstrual bleeding.
Postmenopausal bleeding
Correct. The menstrual history includes intermenstrual and postmenopausal bleeding; in an older woman, any postmenopausal bleeding is a blood loss source to identify.
Pregnancy and recent delivery
Pregnancy and recent delivery are on the history, but are unlikely at 62. Postmenopausal bleeding is the question to ask.
Age at her first period
Age at menarche identifies no source of present blood loss. Postmenopausal bleeding does.

B.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
B.q: When does S4 occur, and what is its cadence?
opts: Early in diastole, with the cadence Ken-TUC-ky
That is S3, the ventricular gallop.
In mid systole, with a clicking quality
A mid to late systolic click comes from mitral valve prolapse.
In very early diastole, with a snapping quality
That is the opening snap of a stenotic mitral valve.
Just before S1, cadence Ten-nes-SEE
Correct — dull and low in pitch, best heard at the apex with the bell in the left lateral decubitus position. It is also called an atrial gallop.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 42

B.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
B.q: Which description fits FINE crackles?
opts: Grating, biphasic, axillary
A grating, biphasic sound best heard in the axilla and lower bases is a pleural rub.
Soft, high-pitched, mid-to-late inspiratory
Correct: fine crackles are softer, higher pitched and very brief, heard mid to late inspiration, especially in dependent lung, and change with body position.
Loud, low-pitched, early inspiratory
Louder, lower-pitched crackles that start early in inspiration and last through expiration are COARSE crackles.
Continuous, musical, expiratory
Continuous musical sounds are wheezes; crackles of either kind are non-musical and discontinuous.

B.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Besides hemolytic anemia, what else causes jaundice?
opts: B12 deficiency
B12 deficiency is known here for its neurologic findings, not jaundice. Disorders of bilirubin metabolism are the other cause.
Bilirubin disorders
Correct. Jaundice and scleral icterus suggest hemolytic anemia, but other causes include disorders of bilirubin metabolism, so the sign is not specific for hemolysis.
Heavy menstrual bleeding
Menstrual blood loss does not cause jaundice. Apart from hemolysis, jaundice comes from disorders of bilirubin metabolism.
Iron deficiency
Iron deficiency is not a jaundice cause; its clues are pica and spoon nails. The other jaundice cause listed is disorders of bilirubin metabolism.

B.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: What may sternal or other bone tenderness suggest in an anemic patient?
opts: A normal finding in adults
Bone tenderness is not normal here: it raises possible marrow disease, though it is nonspecific.
Iron deficiency, specifically
Iron deficiency's clues are spoon nails and hair shedding, not bone tenderness. Bone tenderness points to possible marrow disease.
Hemolysis, specifically
Hemolysis is suggested by jaundice and icterus. Bone tenderness suggests possible marrow disease.
Possible marrow disease
Correct. Sternal or other bone tenderness suggests possible marrow disease but is nonspecific, so other causes must be considered.

B.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
B.q: What is a decrescendo murmur?
opts: One that rises and then falls in intensity
That is crescendo-decrescendo, the diamond shape of aortic and pulmonic stenosis.
One that rises steadily to a peak at S2
A murmur crescendoing up to S2 is the late systolic murmur following a mitral valve prolapse click.
One whose intensity does not change
That is a plateau shape, where the intensity does not change from start to finish.
It begins at maximum and fades to silence
Correct: a decrescendo murmur begins at maximum intensity and grows fainter until it is silent.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 54

B.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
B.q: Which conditions cause a pathologic S3?
opts: Hypertensive heart disease and aortic stenosis
Those cause S4, through ventricular hypertrophy and reduced compliance.
Mitral valve prolapse
That causes a mid to late systolic click with a following murmur.
Pericarditis
That causes a friction rub heard intermittently through both systole and diastole.
Decreased contractility, heart failure, shunts
Correct, with the volume overload coming from aortic or mitral regurgitation — all conditions that raise left ventricular filling pressure. Ventricular volume overload as well.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 40

B.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
B.q: How do patients describe palpitations?
opts: A crushing pressure radiating to the jaw
That describes the character of ischemic chest pain rather than palpitations.
Breathlessness on lying flat
That is orthopnea, which improves when the patient sits up.
Skipping, racing, fluttering, pounding
Correct — an unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat. They may be irregular, may slow or accelerate, or may arise from increased forcefulness of contraction. Or a sense of the heart stopping.
A scratching sensation over the sternum
A scratchy, scraping quality describes the pericardial friction rub heard on auscultation.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 6

B.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
B.q: After chest trauma, a patient has hyperresonance and absent breath sounds on the right, and the trachea is shifted to the left. Which condition fits?
opts: Right tension pneumothorax
Correct: a hyperresonant or tympanic side with absent breath sounds is pneumothorax, and a trachea shifted toward the unaffected side means tension.
Right lower lobe atelectasis
Atelectasis is DULL and pulls the trachea toward the affected right side, not away from it.
Right lobar pneumonia
Pneumonia is dull with increased fremitus and bronchial sounds, and the trachea stays midline.
Right pleural effusion
A large effusion can push the trachea away, but it is DULL to percussion, not hyperresonant.

B.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
B.q: What defines the shape of a murmur?
opts: Where it is loudest on the chest wall
That is location, found by exploring where the murmur is heard loudest.
Its intensity over time
Correct — crescendo-decrescendo is diamond shaped, decrescendo begins at maximum and fades, and plateau does not change.
Whether it is high, medium or low
That is pitch, one of the other seven characteristics.
Whether it radiates elsewhere
Radiation is a separate characteristic from shape, describing where the sound travels.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 54

B.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
B.q: What does an amplitude of 2 plus indicate?
opts: Faint or diminished
That is 1 plus.
Brisk and normal
Correct, on a scale where 4 plus is bounding, 3 plus increased, 1 plus faint or diminished and 0 absent. The standing instruction is to always compare both sides.
Increased
Increased amplitude is graded 3 plus, while 2 plus denotes a brisk and normal pulse.
Bounding
That is 4 plus, the top of the scale.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 86

B.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Which is an example of a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia?
opts: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

This enzyme deficiency is an intrinsic (intracorpuscular) cause of hemolysis, a defect of the red cell itself. Microangiopathic examples are disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
Thalassemia syndromes
Thalassemias are intrinsic hemoglobin defects, not microangiopathic destruction. The microangiopathic examples are disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
Folic acid deficiency
Folic acid deficiency impairs red cell production; it does not destroy red cells. Microangiopathic hemolysis is seen in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Correct. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia is extrinsic red cell destruction, and the examples given are disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
B.q: Where is the dorsalis pedis pulse found?
opts: Dorsum of the foot, lateral to the toe tendon
Correct, and the posterior tibial pulse is found behind the medial malleolus — the two distal pulses used for the ankle brachial index.
Behind the lateral malleolus
The posterior tibial is behind the MEDIAL malleolus; nothing is described behind the lateral.
Behind the medial malleolus
That is the posterior tibial pulse.
In the popliteal fossa
That is the popliteal pulse.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 104

B.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
B.q: Which percussion note over the affected side fits a pneumothorax?
opts: Dull
Dullness means fluid or solid tissue, as in pleural effusion, pneumonia or atelectasis, not air in the pleural space.
Dull with a high diaphragm
Dullness with high diaphragmatic excursion is the pleural effusion pattern.
Resonant and symmetric
Resonant, symmetric notes are the NORMAL finding; a pneumothorax is hyperresonant on one side.
Hyperresonant or tympanic
Correct: a pneumothorax is hyperresonant or tympanic over the affected side, with decreased or absent fremitus and breath sounds.

B.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
B.q: A series of precordial crackles keeps time with the heartbeat rather than with breathing, in a patient with severe central chest pain. What does this suggest?
opts: Inflamed pleura
Inflamed pleura give a pleural rub, which follows respiration and disappears with a breath hold, not the heartbeat.
Interstitial fibrosis
Fibrosis gives fine inspiratory crackles over the lung that follow breathing and change with body position.
Air in the mediastinum
Correct: this is the mediastinal crunch (Hamman sign), from air entering the mediastinum (pneumomediastinum).
Air in the pleural space
A pneumothorax gives decreased or absent breath sounds and hyperresonance, not crackles in time with the heart.

B.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
B.q: Over the left lower chest there is dullness, decreased fremitus and absent breath sounds, with bronchial sounds near the top of the dull area, and the trachea is shifted to the right. Which condition fits?
opts: Left tension pneumothorax
A tension pneumothorax shifts the trachea away too, but it is hyperresonant, not dull.
Left lower lobe atelectasis
Atelectasis pulls the trachea toward the LEFT, the affected side, not to the right.
Left lower lobe pneumonia
Pneumonia is dull too, but it INCREASES fremitus over the area and leaves the trachea midline.
Large left pleural effusion
Correct: a large effusion is dull over the fluid with decreased or absent fremitus and breath sounds, bronchial sounds near its top, and the trachea shifted to the unaffected side.

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
B.q: Dullness to percussion over the lung means what?
opts: The lung is hyperinflated
Hyperinflated lung, as in asthma or obstructive lung disease, gives generalized HYPERRESONANCE, not dullness.
A large air-filled bulla is present
An air-filled bulla gives unilateral hyperresonance; dullness means air has been replaced by fluid or solid tissue.
Fluid or solid tissue has replaced air
Correct: dullness means fluid or solid tissue has replaced the air, as in lobar pneumonia, pleural effusion, hemothorax, empyema, fibrous tissue or tumor.
Air has entered the pleural space
Air in the pleural space (a large pneumothorax) gives UNILATERAL hyperresonance, the opposite of dullness.

B.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Jaundice and scleral icterus in an anemic patient point most toward which mechanism?
opts: Hemolysis
Correct. Jaundice and scleral icterus point to hemolytic anemia, including sickle cell disease. Disorders of bilirubin metabolism are another cause of jaundice.
Renal failure
Renal failure impairs red cell production; it is not the jaundice cause listed. Jaundice points to hemolysis, such as sickle cell disease.
Iron deficiency
Iron deficiency's clues are pica, spoon-shaped nails and hair shedding, not jaundice. Icterus points to hemolysis.
Gastrointestinal blood loss
Blood loss shows in the bleeding history and stool questions. Jaundice with anemia points to hemolysis.

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
B.q: Which breathing pattern is shown?
opts: Cheyne-Stokes breathing
Correct: deep breathing alternates with periods of apnea (no breathing), the waxing and waning pattern of Cheyne-Stokes breathing.
Ataxic (Biot) breathing
Ataxic (Biot) breathing is IRREGULAR, with apnea alternating with deep breaths that stop suddenly, not a smooth rise and fall.
Obstructive breathing
Obstructive breathing is prolonged expiration from narrowed airways, without the periods of apnea seen here.
Sighing respiration
Sighing respiration is breathing interrupted by frequent sighs, with no stretches of apnea between the breaths.
B.alt: Breathing tracing in which the breaths grow deeper (labeled hyperpnea) and then fade into a flat line (labeled apnea) before the cycle repeats.

B.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
B.q: When does S3 occur, and how is it best heard?
opts: In very early diastole, with the diaphragm
A very early diastolic sound best heard with the diaphragm is an opening snap.
Just before S1, with the bell at the apex
That is S4, the atrial gallop, whose cadence is Ten-nes-SEE.
In mid systole, with the diaphragm at the base
A midsystolic sound at the base would be an ejection sound or murmur rather than S3.
Early in diastole, with the bell at the apex
Correct, with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. The cadence is Ken-TUC-ky, and it is also called a ventricular gallop.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 40

B.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
B.q: Which feature fits a pleural rub?
opts: Loudest over the neck
The neck is where stridor is heard; a pleural rub is best heard in the axilla and lower bases.
Clears after the patient coughs
A pleural rub is NOT affected by coughing; sounds that clear with coughing are rhonchi from secretions.
Keeps time with the heartbeat
Keeping time with the heartbeat describes the mediastinal crunch, not the respiratory pleural rub.
Louder with firm stethoscope pressure
Correct: a pleural rub increases with firm stethoscope pressure, is not affected by coughing, and disappears with a breath hold.

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
B.q: Which chest deformity distorts the underlying lungs enough to make lung findings very difficult to interpret?
opts: Thoracic kyphoscoliosis
Correct: abnormal spinal curvature and vertebral rotation deform the chest, and the distorted lungs make findings very difficult to interpret.
Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Funnel chest is a depressed lower sternum that may cause murmurs; kyphoscoliosis is the one that distorts lung findings.
Barrel chest
Barrel chest is an increased anteroposterior diameter, normal in infancy and common with aging; it is not the one singled out for distorting findings.
Pigeon chest (pectus carinatum)
Pigeon chest is a forward-displaced sternum; the deformity that distorts the lungs and their findings is kyphoscoliosis.

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
B.q: The cross-section and the front view show the same chest. Which deformity is it?
opts: Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Correct: the lower portion of the sternum is depressed; compression of the heart and great vessels may cause murmurs.
Pigeon chest (pectus carinatum)
Pigeon chest is the opposite: the sternum is displaced ANTERIORLY with the adjacent costal cartilages depressed.
Traumatic flail chest
Flail chest is paradoxical movement of a segment after multiple rib fractures, not a fixed depression of the sternum.
Barrel chest
Barrel chest is an increased anteroposterior diameter with a rounded cross-section, not a sunken lower sternum.
B.alt: Outline of a chest cross-section with a dip in the front at the sternum, beside a view of a young man's chest with a hollow over the lower breastbone.

B.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
B.q: Which murmurs does isometric handgrip increase?
opts: Aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Those two are distinguished by the preload maneuvers of Valsalva, standing and squatting.
Tricuspid regurgitation only
Tricuspid regurgitation is not in the handgrip list; handgrip increases mitral and aortic regurgitation.
Mitral regurgitation and aortic regurgitation
Correct, because handgrip raises left-sided afterload. It also increases the murmurs of ventricular septal defect and mitral stenosis, a different set from the preload maneuvers.
The pericardial friction rub
A friction rub is not a murmur and is not in the handgrip list, which includes mitral and aortic regurgitation.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 63

B.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
B.q: Which adventitious sound is continuous and musical, produced by rapid airflow through bronchi narrowed almost to closure?
opts: Coarse crackles
Coarse crackles are non-musical and discontinuous, with a popping sound from larger airway secretions or fluid.
Wheezes
Correct: wheezes are continuous musical sounds from rapid airflow through bronchial airways narrowed almost to the point of closure; typical of asthma.
Pleural rub
A pleural rub is a discontinuous, low-frequency grating sound from inflamed pleura, not a musical airway sound.
Stridor
Stridor is musical too, but it comes from a narrowing in the UPPER respiratory tract and is best heard over the neck.

B.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
B.q: Which symptom in an anemic patient most strongly suggests SEVERE anemia?
opts: Weakness
Weakness and reduced exercise tolerance are common symptoms, listed with fatigue. The ones that mark severe anemia are syncope, chest pain and symptoms at rest.
Hair shedding
Hair shedding is a possible iron deficiency clue with many other causes; it says nothing about severity. Syncope, chest pain and rest symptoms do.
Fatigue
Fatigue is the most common symptom and appears even with mild anemia, so it does not mark severity. Syncope, chest pain and symptoms at rest do.
Syncope
Correct. Symptoms at rest, chest pain and syncope are the severity markers; patients with them need urgent assessment. Fatigue and weakness are common even in mild anemia.

B.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
B.q: A wheeze is heard over only one area of the lung. What may cause a localized wheeze?
opts: Pulmonary or interstitial fibrosis
Fibrosis gives fine crackles, soft and high-pitched in mid-to-late inspiration, not a localized wheeze.
A foreign body, mucous plug or tumor
Correct: wheezes may be localized from a foreign body, mucous plug or tumor, or heard throughout the lung, as in asthma.
Laryngeal edema or epiglottitis
Narrowing in the larynx or upper airway produces stridor over the neck, not a wheeze over one area of lung.
Pleural effusion or pneumothorax
Effusion and pneumothorax DECREASE or abolish breath sounds; they do not produce a localized wheeze.

B.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
B.q: How do coarse crackles differ from fine crackles?
opts: They are continuous and musical
Both kinds of crackle are non-musical and discontinuous; continuous musical sounds are wheezes.
They do not change with body position
Correct: coarse crackles are louder, lower in pitch, start early in inspiration and last through expiration, and do not change with position (larger airway secretions or fluid).
They disappear when the breath is held
Disappearing with a breath hold separates a pleural RUB from a pericardial friction rub; it does not separate crackles.
They are higher pitched and softer
That reverses them: coarse crackles are LOUDER and LOWER in pitch; fine crackles are the soft, high-pitched ones.

B.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
B.q: What is the duration of a normal hyperkinetic left ventricular impulse?
opts: Less than two thirds of systole
Correct, against a sustained duration in pressure overload and an often slightly sustained one in volume overload.
Sustained through systole
A sustained duration is the pressure overload pattern, seen in aortic stenosis and hypertension.
Continuous through systole and diastole
A sound heard through both phases describes the pericardial friction rub rather than an impulse.
Confined to diastole
The ventricular impulse occurs during contraction, which is systole.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 23

B.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Besides fatigue and weakness, which symptom belongs to the general symptoms of anemia?
opts: Melena
Melena, black tarry stool, is part of the bleeding history: a clue to a gastrointestinal source, not a general symptom. Exertional dyspnea is a general symptom.
Pica
Pica, especially chewing ice, points to iron deficiency, a specific cause. The general symptoms include exertional dyspnea and palpitations.
Exertional dyspnea
Correct. The general symptoms are fatigue, weakness, exertional dyspnea, palpitations and lightheadedness. They establish anemia's effect but do not point to its cause.
Paresthesias
Paresthesias are a clue to B12 deficiency, a specific cause. The general symptoms are fatigue, weakness, exertional dyspnea, palpitations and lightheadedness.

B.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Which group of clues points to B12 deficiency?
opts: Pica, brittle nails and hair shedding
Pica, brittle or spoon-shaped nails and hair shedding are the IRON deficiency clues. B12 deficiency is neurologic: paresthesias, balance, vibration and position sense.
Paresthesias, poor balance, lost vibration
Correct. The B12 clues are paresthesias, impaired balance and reduced vibration or position sense.
Easy bruising, nosebleeds and gum bleeding
These belong to the bleeding history. B12 deficiency shows instead as paresthesias, impaired balance and reduced vibration or position sense.
Bloating, chronic diarrhea and weight loss
These suggest possible malabsorption, a risk factor rather than the deficiency's own signs. B12 deficiency gives paresthesias, poor balance and lost vibration sense.

B.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Which surgical history is a risk factor for iron or B12 deficiency?
opts: Cholecystectomy
Gallbladder removal is not among the listed risks. Gastric bypass, gastrectomy and intestinal resection are, because they impair absorption.
Knee replacement
Orthopedic surgery does not impair nutrient absorption. Gastric bypass, gastrectomy and intestinal resection do, and belong in the history.
Gastric bypass
Correct. Gastric bypass, gastrectomy and intestinal resection are listed risks: they impair absorption, so a patient can be deficient despite a good diet.
Appendectomy
An appendectomy does not appear among the risks. The surgeries that matter are gastric bypass, gastrectomy and intestinal resection, which impair absorption.

B.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
B.q: A witnessed apnea is a cessation of breathing lasting at least how long?
opts: 5 seconds
Five seconds is too short; a witnessed apnea is a pause of 10 seconds or more.
10 seconds
Correct: an apnea is breathing cessation for 10 seconds or more, as witnessed by someone in the household.
30 seconds
The threshold is lower: breathing cessation for 10 seconds or more counts as an apnea.
60 seconds
