A full minute far exceeds the threshold; an apnea is a pause of 10 seconds or more.

B.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Which menstrual history detail helps judge how heavy a patient's bleeding is?
opts: Flooding and protection changes
Correct. The menstrual history asks duration, flooding, protection changes and daily impact, and any intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding.
The brand of protection used
The brand does not matter; how often protection is changed does. Ask also about duration, flooding and daily impact.
Age at the first period
Age at menarche does not measure loss. The menstrual history asks duration, flooding, protection changes and daily impact.
Whether cramps are present
Cramping is not on the list. Heaviness is judged by duration, flooding, protection changes and daily impact.

B.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Which three sources of blood loss are named as causes of anemia?
opts: Gastrointestinal, lupus and transfusion
Gastrointestinal loss belongs here, but lupus and transfusion reactions are extrinsic causes of hemolysis. The blood loss trio is trauma, menstrual and gastrointestinal.
Menstrual, malaria and chronic disease
Menstrual loss belongs here, but malaria causes hemolysis and chronic disease impairs production. Blood loss is trauma, menstrual or gastrointestinal.
Trauma, menstrual and gastrointestinal
Correct. Blood loss anemia is traced to trauma, menstrual loss or the gastrointestinal tract, which is why the bleeding and menstrual history and the stool questions matter.
Trauma, hemolysis and renal failure
Trauma is a blood loss source, but hemolysis is destruction and renal failure is impaired production. The other two blood loss sources are menstrual and gastrointestinal.

B.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
B.q: After surgery and days of immobility, a patient develops sudden, unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis and a swollen leg. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Left-sided heart failure
Heart failure brings orthopnea, edema and weight gain, worse lying flat; sudden hemoptysis after immobility is embolic.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is sudden with unilateral pleuritic pain, but hemoptysis and a swollen leg are not part of its pattern.
Pulmonary embolism
Correct: sudden unexplained dyspnea with pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, syncope or unilateral leg symptoms, after surgery or immobility, is pulmonary embolism.
Pneumonia
Pneumonia is acute with fever, chills, cough and sputum; the immobility and swollen leg point to an embolism.

B.io: Review the point of maximal impulse and apical impulse
B.q: What is the normal diameter and quality of the point of maximal impulse?
opts: About 1 cm, faint and barely palpable
The normal impulse is usually palpated as brisk and tapping at about 2.5 cm.
About 5 cm, diffuse and sustained
A diffuse impulse much larger than the size of a quarter suggests ventricular dilation from chronic volume overload; a normal impulse is only about 2.5 cm.
Too variable to have a normal value
A normal supine diameter of about 2.5 cm is given, roughly the size of a quarter, brisk and tapping.
About 2.5 cm, brisk and tapping
Correct, measured with the patient supine — about the size of a quarter.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 20

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
B.q: How should the patient be prepared before brachial pressure is measured for an ankle brachial index?
opts: Supine and resting for ten minutes
Correct, and the cuff is inflated 20 mm Hg above the last audible pulse then deflated at about 1 mm Hg per second, with two measurements averaged in each arm.
Immediately on arrival, with no rest
A ten minute supine rest is specified before the brachial pressure is taken.
Standing for two minutes
Standing would alter the pressures; the patient is supine and resting.
Seated with feet flat for five minutes
The patient is supine for ten minutes rather than seated, since posture alters the pressure.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 111

B.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
B.q: Which maneuvers increase the murmur of mitral regurgitation?
opts: Valsalva or standing
Those reduce preload and are used to bring out hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Leaning forward after full exhalation
That position brings out aortic regurgitation and the pericardial friction rub.
Handgrip or squatting
Correct, both of which increase the resistance the left ventricle works against or the volume it handles.
Inspiration
Slight increase with inspiration is characteristic of tricuspid regurgitation, a right-sided murmur.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 74

B.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
B.q: How does the location of the left ventricular impulse differ in volume overload?
opts: Displaced medially toward the sternum
Volume overload displaces the impulse laterally rather than medially.
Moved to the subxiphoid process
A subxiphoid location is described for the RIGHT ventricular impulse.
Unchanged from normal
Location stays normal in the hyperkinetic and pressure-overload patterns, not in volume overload.
Displaced to the left and possibly downward
Correct, whereas in hyperkinetic and pressure-overload states the location stays normal — so displacement is what distinguishes dilation from hypertrophy.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 23

B.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: What does this picture show at the corners of the mouth?
opts: Palatal petechiae
Palatal petechiae are on the roof of the mouth. The finding is at the corners: angular cheilitis.
Angular cheilitis
Correct. Inflammation and fissures at the corners of the mouth are angular cheilitis. Causes include nutritional deficiency, Candida, bacteria and local irritation.
Glossitis
Glossitis is a smooth, sore, beefy-red tongue. The cracks here are at the mouth corners.
Oral mucosal pallor
Pallor is a pale mucosa. This shows fissures at the corners of the mouth.
B.alt: Close view of a woman's closed lips with pale, cracked fissures at both corners of the mouth.

B.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
B.q: Massive hemoptysis is defined as more than how much blood in 24 hours?
opts: More than 100 mL
The threshold is far higher: massive hemoptysis is more than 600 mL in 24 hours.
More than 300 mL
Massive hemoptysis is more than 600 mL in 24 hours, twice this volume.
More than 600 mL
Correct: more than 600 mL in 24 hours is massive hemoptysis, which can be life threatening and requires urgent intervention.
More than 1,000 mL
The cut-off is lower: more than 600 mL in 24 hours already counts as massive and needs urgent intervention.

B.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
B.q: A patient reports musical breathing sounds that others can hear. What produces this symptom?
opts: Partial lower airway obstruction
Correct: wheezing comes from partial lower airway obstruction, by secretions and tissue inflammation in asthma or by a foreign body.
Small airways snapping open
Deflated small airways snapping open on inspiration produce crackles, which are NON-musical and discontinuous.
Inflamed pleura rubbing together
Roughened pleural surfaces sliding together produce a grating pleural rub, not a musical sound.
Fluid in the pleural space
Fluid in the pleural space is a pleural effusion: dull to percussion, with decreased or absent breath sounds rather than a musical sound.

B.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: How do Cullen and Grey Turner signs typically behave?
opts: Uncommon, and may appear late
Correct. Both signs are uncommon findings with a possible delayed appearance, so their absence does not exclude significant bleeding.
Seen only with minor bleeding
They are signs of internal bleeding (or severe pancreatitis), not of minor bleeding; they are uncommon and may appear late.
Common, and appear within minutes
They are uncommon and may be delayed, not common and immediate. Absent signs do not exclude significant bleeding.
Present in every internal bleed
They are uncommon findings: significant bleeding is still possible without them.

B.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
B.q: In which group is hemoptysis rare?
opts: Adults with tuberculosis
Pulmonary tuberculosis is a listed cause of hemoptysis; it is rare in infants, children and adolescents.
Adults with lung cancer
Lung cancer is a listed cause of hemoptysis; the group in which it is rare is infants, children and adolescents.
Adults with bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis is one of the listed causes of hemoptysis, so it is not the group in which hemoptysis is rare.
Infants, children and adolescents
Correct: hemoptysis is rare in infants, children and adolescents; its listed causes are adult lung diseases such as tuberculosis and lung cancer.

B.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Which chronic condition belongs in the medical history of an anemic patient?
opts: Chronic kidney disease
Correct. The medical history covers chronic kidney disease, inflammatory disease, liver disease and malignancy; renal failure and chronic disease impair red cell production.
Seasonal allergies
Allergies are not part of it. Ask about chronic kidney disease, inflammatory disease, liver disease and malignancy.
Myopia
Myopia has no bearing on red cell production. The list is chronic kidney disease, inflammatory disease, liver disease and malignancy.
Migraine
Migraine is not on the hematologic medical history. Chronic kidney, inflammatory and liver disease and malignancy are.

B.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
B.q: When does paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea typically occur?
opts: One to two hours after going to bed
Correct — episodes of sudden dyspnea and orthopnea that wake the patient, prompting them to sit up, stand, or go to a window for air. Wheezing and coughing may accompany it.
Immediately on lying down
Breathlessness immediately on lying supine describes orthopnea rather than the paroxysmal nocturnal form.
Only during exertion
Exertional breathlessness is ordinary dyspnea; this occurs at rest, during sleep.
In the early morning on waking
The episodes wake the patient from sleep rather than occurring on natural waking.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 7

B.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
B.q: Besides nutritional deficiency, what else can cause angular cheilitis?
opts: Nitrous oxide exposure
Nitrous oxide is not among the listed causes of angular cheilitis: nutritional deficiency, Candida, bacteria and local irritation.
Hemolysis
Hemolysis gives jaundice and icterus. Angular cheilitis can come from Candida, bacteria or local irritation as well as deficiency.
Candida infection
Correct. Angular cheilitis can come from nutritional deficiency, Candida, bacteria or local irritation, which is why it is nonspecific.
Lead exposure
Lead is not among the listed causes of angular cheilitis. Those are nutritional deficiency, Candida, bacteria and local irritation.

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
B.q: What percussion note does healthy lung produce?
opts: Resonant
Correct: healthy lung is resonant; dullness means fluid or solid tissue has replaced air, and hyperresonance means extra air.
Hyperresonant
Hyperresonance is generalized over the hyperinflated lungs of asthma or obstructive lung disease, or unilateral with a pneumothorax.
Tympanic
A tympanic note over the chest is a pneumothorax finding on the affected side; healthy lung is resonant.
Dull
Dullness means fluid or solid tissue has replaced the air in the lung, as in lobar pneumonia or pleural effusion.

B.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
B.q: Which group is most likely to report atypical symptoms in acute coronary syndrome?
opts: Men over 65
Men with acute coronary syndrome most often describe the classic symptoms of exertional angina, rather than atypical symptoms.
Men under 40
Men with acute coronary syndrome most often describe classic symptoms of exertional angina; women over 65 are the group with atypical symptoms.
Women over 65

Correct — upper back, neck and jaw pain, shortness of breath, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, nausea, vomiting and fatigue. Men and women otherwise most often describe classic symptoms of exertional angina.
Women under 40
Younger women are not the group named: women over 65 report atypical symptoms such as upper back, neck and jaw pain.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 5

B.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
B.q: Describe the murmur of mitral regurgitation.
opts: Early diastolic, decrescendo, high frequency
That describes aortic regurgitation.
Midsystolic in the aortic area, crescendo-decrescendo
That describes aortic stenosis.
Pansystolic at the lower left sternal border, blowing
That describes tricuspid regurgitation, which does not radiate to the axilla.
Pansystolic at the apex, harsh
Correct, radiating to the left axilla, with an apical thrill if loud. The harshness is attributed to the left ventricle being the powerful chamber. The frequency is medium to high.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 74

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
B.q: Which chest wall deformity do these two views show?
opts: Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Funnel chest is the reverse: a depression in the lower sternum rather than a sternum pushed forward.
Thoracic kyphoscoliosis
Kyphoscoliosis is a curvature and rotation of the spine that deforms the chest; the sternum is not pushed forward.
Pigeon chest (pectus carinatum)
Correct: the sternum is displaced anteriorly, increasing the anteroposterior diameter, and the costal cartilages next to it are depressed.
Barrel chest
Barrel chest raises the anteroposterior diameter evenly with a rounded outline, without a forward-pointing sternum.
B.alt: Outline of a chest cross-section that comes to a point at the front, with the sternum pushed forward and the cartilages beside it pressed in, beside a side view of a boy's chest.

B.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
B.q: How is dyspnea defined?
opts: Pain on deep inspiration from the pleura
Pain with deep inspiration is pleuritic pain from the parietal pleura; dyspnea is defined as PAINLESS.
Rapid, shallow breathing at rest
Rapid, shallow breathing is the tachypnea pattern seen on inspection; dyspnea is the patient's uncomfortable awareness of breathing.
A pause in breathing during sleep
A pause in breathing of 10 seconds or more is a witnessed apnea, asked about in disordered sleep, not the definition of dyspnea.
Breathing awareness out of proportion to exertion
Correct: dyspnea is a painless but uncomfortable awareness of breathing that is inappropriate to the level of exertion.

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
B.q: Hyperresonance on only ONE side of the chest suggests which?
opts: A hemothorax or an empyema
Blood or pus in the chest replaces air and gives DULLNESS, not hyperresonance.
A large pneumothorax or air-filled bulla
Correct: unilateral hyperresonance suggests a large pneumothorax or an air-filled bulla; generalized hyperresonance suggests hyperinflation.
Hyperinflation from asthma
Asthma and obstructive lung disease hyperinflate BOTH lungs and give generalized, not unilateral, hyperresonance.
A tumor or fibrous tissue
Tumor and fibrous tissue are solid and give dullness to percussion rather than hyperresonance.

B.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
B.q: Which chemical is asked about as a marrow-toxic exposure?
opts: Nitrous oxide
Nitrous oxide is linked to B12 deficiency, not named as marrow-toxic. Benzene is the marrow-toxic chemical.
Benzene
Correct. Benzene and other marrow-toxic chemicals are on the exposure history, beside lead from renovation work and pre-1978 buildings.
Chlorine
Chlorine is not on the exposure history. Benzene and other marrow-toxic chemicals are.
Lead
Lead is asked about too, but as its own exposure (renovation, pre-1978 buildings). The listed marrow-toxic chemical is benzene.

B.io: Review the point of maximal impulse and apical impulse
B.q: Where may the point of maximal impulse shift in cardiomegaly?
opts: More medial, toward the sternum
Enlargement moves the left border outward rather than inward.
More lateral, and possibly inferior
Correct — the sixth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line is given as an example. The instruction is to DOCUMENT where you palpate it.
Superiorly, to the second intercostal space
The shift described is lateral and possibly inferior.
It does not move with a change in heart size
It marks the left border of the heart, so a change in size or shape moves it.
B.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 20

B.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
B.q: Irregular breathing in which apnea alternates with deep breaths that stop suddenly describes which pattern?
opts: Ataxic (Biot) breathing
Correct: ataxic (Biot) breathing is irregular, with apnea alternating with deep breaths that stop suddenly.
Bradypnea
Bradypnea is slow breathing, with or without increased tidal volume, not an irregular pattern broken by apnea.
Sighing respiration
Sighing respiration is breathing interrupted by frequent sighs; occasional sighs are normal, and there are no apneas.
Cheyne-Stokes breathing
Cheyne-Stokes breathing is a regular cycle of deep breathing alternating with apnea, not an irregular pattern of breaths that stop suddenly.

B.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
B.q: What is the most common cause of syncope?
opts: Aortic stenosis
Valve disease can cause syncope but is not named as the commonest cause.
Arrhythmia
A cardiac origin from arrhythmia accounts for about 20 percent, so it is the minority rather than the most common cause.
Neurocardiogenic, also called vasovagal
Correct, with a cardiac origin from arrhythmias in about 20 percent of cases. Syncope itself is transient loss of consciousness followed by recovery.
Orthostatic hypotension
The cause named as most common is neurocardiogenic, or vasovagal, syncope.

B.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders

Cold and pale

It is left out of the history

As risk information; hemoglobinopathies occur in any ancestry

C.q: After multiple rib fractures, one area of the chest wall moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration. What is this?

Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Funnel chest is a fixed depression of the lower sternum, present at rest, not a segment that moves the wrong way with each breath.
Unilateral respiratory lag

Traumatic flail chest

Correct: multiple rib fractures can cause paradoxical movement: as the diaphragm descends and intrathoracic pressure falls on inspiration, the injured area caves inward, and on expiration it moves outward.

C.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
C.q: A patient's skin, conjunctivae and nail beds look entirely normal. What does this mean for anemia?
opts: Severe anemia is excluded
Even severe anemia is not ruled out by appearance; severity is judged from symptoms and vital signs. Anemia is still possible.
Anemia is excluded
A normal look cannot exclude anemia. Pallor is unreliable both ways, so anemia is still possible.
Anemia is still possible
Correct. A normal appearance does not exclude anemia: anemia is still possible. Pallor itself is an unreliable estimate of the hemoglobin.
The anemia must be from hemolysis
A normal appearance does not point to any one mechanism. It simply leaves anemia possible.

C.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
C.q: Which questions help characterize edema?
opts: How far can you walk before the pain stops you?

Walking distance before pain describes claudication, pain with walking that can progress to pain at rest in chronic arterial insufficiency, which has no edema. Edema questions ask about swelling: where, when and in what setting. The tell: this question is about pain with exercise, while edema questions are about tightness and puffiness.
Does the sensation feel like skipping or fluttering?

'Skipping' and 'fluttering' are the words patients use for palpitations, an unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat, not for swelling. Palpitations do not necessarily mean heart disease and are followed up with an electrocardiogram. The tell: this asks how the heartbeat feels, while edema questions ask where the body swells and when.
Do shoes or rings get tight? Eyelids puffy?

Correct. Edema questions focus on the location, timing and setting of the swelling and on associated symptoms, and tight shoes, tight rings and puffy eyelids in the morning ask exactly where and when the fluid collects. Asking whether it is worse in the morning or the evening, and suggesting a daily morning weight, round out the history.
How many pillows do you sleep on?

Pillow count quantifies orthopnea, dyspnea that comes on lying supine and improves on sitting up, not swelling. Edema is excess fluid in the extravascular interstitial space and is asked about by location, timing and setting. The tell: pillows measure breathing while lying flat; tight shoes and rings measure fluid in the tissues.

C.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
C.q: Sharp chest pain is worse with inspiration and cough, is not reproduced by pressing on the chest, and does not ease when sitting forward. Which pattern is this?
opts: Positional
The sharp positional pattern is worse supine and IMPROVED by sitting forward (pericarditis); this pain did not ease sitting forward.
Reproducible
Localized, reproducible pain is provoked by movement or palpation with focal tenderness (chest wall pain); pressing did not reproduce this.
Postprandial
Burning postprandial pain is worse after meals, bending over or lying down (esophageal disease), not with inspiration and cough.
Pleuritic
Correct: sharp pain worse with inspiration or cough is the pleuritic pattern, which points to pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia or pleuritis.

C.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
C.q: Chest pain began abruptly, was at its worst from the start, and radiates to the back. Which diagnosis does this pattern suggest?
opts: Myocardial infarction
Infarction gives retrosternal pressure or squeezing, often exertional, radiating to the arm, neck, jaw or back, not maximal at onset.
Aortic dissection
Correct: sudden, tearing pain that is maximal early and radiates to the back is the pattern listed for aortic dissection.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is sudden too, but its pain is sharp and pleuritic, worse with inspiration or cough, rather than tearing to the back.
Pericarditis
Pericarditis is sharp and positional, worse supine and improved sitting forward, not abrupt tearing pain.

C.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
C.q: During Romberg testing, a patient becomes much more unsteady when the eyes close. What does this suggest?
opts: Hemolysis
Romberg does not test for hemolysis. Greater instability with eye closure suggests impaired proprioception.
A normal response
A marked increase in unsteadiness with the eyes closed is the abnormal finding: impaired proprioception.
Iron deficiency
Romberg tests proprioception, not a blood-cell cause: greater instability with eye closure suggests impaired proprioception, not iron deficiency.
Impaired proprioception
Correct. Greater instability with eye closure suggests impaired proprioception, as in posterior column involvement from B12 deficiency.

Sleep loss is a consequence rather than the measure; pillow count or sleeping upright is what quantifies it.
By how far the patient can walk before stopping

By the oxygen saturation when lying flat
The quantification described is by pillow count rather than by saturation.
By the number of pillows used for sleeping

Sixth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
That is where it may shift TO when the heart enlarges, rather than the normal position.
Fifth space, at or just medial to midclavicular

The aortic ejection sound does not vary with respiration while the pulmonic one decreases on inspiration.

C.q: What is the usual ratio of anteroposterior to lateral chest diameter in an adult?

The chest is deeper than that: the anteroposterior diameter is usually 0.7 to 0.9 of the lateral diameter.
About 0.7 to 0.9

About 1.1 to 1.3

Caffeine intake after noon

C.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
C.q: How do rhonchi differ from wheezes?
opts: Grating; vanish when the breath is held
A grating sound that vanishes with a breath hold is a pleural rub, not rhonchi.
Discontinuous; from airways snapping open
Discontinuous sounds from small airways snapping open are crackles; rhonchi are continuous, like wheezes.
Lower in pitch; may clear with coughing
Correct: rhonchi are a variant of wheezes, lower in pitch, and may disappear with coughing, so secretions may be involved.
Higher in pitch; heard on inspiration

C.q: What defines a pansystolic murmur?
opts: It begins after a click in mid systole
That is a late systolic murmur, following a mitral valve prolapse click.
It spans both systole and diastole
A sound heard through both is a continuous murmur or a pericardial friction rub.
It occupies the middle of systole only
That is a midsystolic murmur, which may be innocent, physiologic or pathologic.
It begins with S1 and continues to S2
Correct — something is open through all of systole, with blood flowing from a high pressure chamber to a lower one through a structure that should be closed. All are pathologic.

C.q: Which spinal cord structures are affected in B12 deficiency?
opts: Spinothalamic and spinocerebellar tracts
These are not the tracts named. B12 deficiency involves the posterior columns and the lateral corticospinal tracts.
Anterior horns and spinothalamic tracts
Neither the anterior horns nor the spinothalamic tracts are the named sites. B12 deficiency affects the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.
Cerebellum and basal ganglia
These are not spinal cord structures. The ataxia of B12 deficiency is SENSORY, from the posterior columns, with the lateral corticospinal tracts also affected.
Posterior columns, corticospinal tracts
Correct. B12 deficiency affects the posterior columns (impaired vibration and position sense) and the lateral corticospinal tracts (possible spasticity and hyperreflexia).

C.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
C.q: How do diastolic murmurs compare with systolic ones?
opts: Less common and more difficult to hear

Correct. Diastolic murmurs are both less common than systolic murmurs and more difficult to hear, which answers both halves of the comparison the stem asks for. That is why they need deliberate technique: aortic regurgitation, for example, is grade 1 to 3, high-pitched and heard best with the patient sitting, leaning forward and holding the breath after exhaling.
Always pathologic and always loud

Diastolic murmurs are not described as loud: they are more difficult to hear than systolic ones, and aortic regurgitation, for example, is only grade 1 to 3 and may be mistaken for breath sounds. The tell: 'always' appears twice, when the defining fact about diastolic murmurs is that they are less common and easy to miss.
More common and easier to hear

This reverses both halves of the comparison: diastolic murmurs are less common than systolic murmurs and more difficult to hear, so the systolic group is the commoner, louder one. The tell: a soft, high-pitched diastolic murmur such as aortic regurgitation can be mistaken for breath sounds, the opposite of easy to hear.
Equally common but louder

Both halves are off: diastolic murmurs are less common than systolic murmurs, not equally common, and harder to hear rather than louder. Aortic regurgitation, a typical one, is a soft decrescendo murmur of grade 1 to 3. The tell: a louder murmur would not need the patient leaning forward with the breath held after exhaling to be heard.

C.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
C.q: Which nail finding defines clubbing?

Loss of the nail-to-fold angle
Correct: clubbing is a bulbous swelling at the nail base with loss of the normal angle between the nail and the proximal nail fold.
A hard, fixed nail bed
The clubbed nail bed is the opposite: it feels spongy or floating, with loss of the nail-to-fold angle.
Blue color of the nail beds

The attack is beginning to resolve

A silent chest needing immediate action

Just medial to the apex, and the lower sternal border

At the subxiphoid process

C.q: An anemic patient's stool blood test is negative. What can be concluded?

Gastrointestinal bleeding is excluded

Further evaluation can stop

Gastrointestinal bleeding is still possible

C.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
C.q: What is a bruit?
opts: A high-pitched sound from a stenotic mitral valve opening

A high-pitched sound as a stenotic mitral valve opens is the opening snap, a very early diastolic sound of cardiac origin. A bruit is defined by the opposite origin: vascular, not cardiac. The tell: the opening snap is heard just medial to the apex, while bruits are listened for over the aorta and the renal, iliac and femoral arteries.
A murmur-like sound of vascular origin

Correct. A bruit is a murmur-like sound of vascular rather than cardiac origin, the distinction the stem's definition turns on. You listen for it over the aorta in the abdominal midline, the renal arteries 3 to 4 centimeters lateral to the aorta, the iliac arteries lateral to and below the umbilicus, and directly over the femoral arteries.
A scratchy sound from pericardial inflammation

A scratchy sound from pericardial inflammation is the pericardial friction rub of pericarditis, which is cardiac in origin and most often heard at Erb's point. A bruit comes from a blood vessel, not the sac around the heart. The tell: the rub is heard over the chest, while bruits are heard over the arteries of the abdomen and groin.
A palpable vibration from a loud murmur

A palpable vibration from a loud murmur is a thrill, felt with the balls of the hand pressed against the chest wall, not heard. A bruit is something you auscultate over an artery. The tell: a thrill is felt by touch over the heart, while a bruit is a sound over a vessel such as the aorta or a renal, iliac or femoral artery.

C.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
C.q: A hospitalized patient is too weak to sit up for the posterior chest examination. How should the back be examined?
opts: Roll the patient to one side, then the other
Correct: the posterior chest is ideally examined sitting, arms folded; if that cannot be done, roll the patient to one side and then the other, percussing and auscultating in each position.
Examine the anterior chest and skip the back
The posterior chest is not skipped; rolling the patient to each side lets you percuss and auscultate the back in turn.
Auscultate the back through the gown
Clothes and paper gowns produce sounds, so the patient is de-robed; rolling to each side gives access to the back.
Wait until the patient can sit upright
There is no need to defer: rolling the patient to one side, then the other, completes the posterior examination.

C.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
C.q: Which chest wall deformity may compress the heart and great vessels and cause murmurs?
opts: Pigeon chest (pectus carinatum)
Pigeon chest pushes the sternum forward, away from the heart, so it is not the deformity linked to murmurs.
Barrel chest
Barrel chest is an increased anteroposterior diameter, normal in infancy and common with aging and obstructive lung disease.
Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Correct: in funnel chest the lower sternum is depressed, and compression of the heart and great vessels may cause murmurs.
Traumatic flail chest
Flail chest is paradoxical movement of a fractured rib segment, not compression of the heart.

C.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
C.q: When taking an anemia history, what should be compared with the patient's current symptoms?
opts: Their oxygen saturation
Oxygen saturation is not what the history compares with the symptoms; they are compared with the patient's own baseline function, onset and progression.
Their baseline function
Correct. The history covers onset, progression and change from baseline function: what the patient could do before and what they can no longer do as easily.
Their family's symptoms
Family history is asked for hemoglobinopathy, bleeding and jaundice, but symptoms are measured against the patient's own baseline function.
A standard hemoglobin chart
Hemoglobin thresholds define anemia; the history compares symptoms with the patient's own baseline function, their onset and progression.

C.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
C.q: Cyanosis of the lips, tongue and oral mucosa signals what?
opts: Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis is associated with clubbing of the nails, not defined by cyanosis of the lips and tongue, which signals hypoxia.
Acute coronary syndrome
Pallor and diaphoresis are the color changes common in acute coronary syndrome and heart failure; central cyanosis signals hypoxia.
Hypoxia
Correct: cyanosis in the lips, tongue and oral mucosa signals hypoxia, and is looked for with skin and nail color during the survey.
Upper airway obstruction
Upper airway obstruction is signaled by stridor, a high-pitched inspiratory whistle over the neck, not by cyanosis as such.

C.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
C.q: What are petechiae?
opts: Pinpoint, nonblanching skin hemorrhages
Correct. Petechiae are pinpoint, nonblanching skin hemorrhages. Purpura are larger nonblanching lesions, and ecchymoses are larger areas of bruising.
Larger nonblanching hemorrhagic lesions
Larger nonblanching hemorrhagic lesions are purpura. Petechiae are the pinpoint ones.
Larger areas of bruising
Larger areas of bruising are ecchymoses. Petechiae are pinpoint, nonblanching hemorrhages.
Small red spots that blanch with pressure
Petechiae are NONblanching; that is what marks them as hemorrhage into the skin.

C.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
C.q: What is melena?
opts: Blood or coffee-ground emesis
Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material is hematemesis. Melena refers to the stool: black and tarry.
Red or maroon blood per rectum

Blood in the urine

Black, tarry stool

Number of siblings

Preferred exercise

opts: Excess fluid within the vascular compartment
The accumulation is EXTRAvascular, in the interstitial space.
Excess fluid in the extravascular interstitial space
Correct, and the striking figure is that up to 10 percent of body weight can accumulate before pitting edema appears.
Dilated tortuous superficial veins
Those are varicosities, a mild to severe dilatation of veins mainly in the lower extremities.
Brown discoloration of the lower leg
Hemosiderin staining is a skin change of chronic venous insufficiency rather than the definition of edema.

Restless leg syndrome is listed as a different cause of disordered sleep, not the hallmark of obstructive sleep apnea.
Loud, persistent snoring at night

Waking with a morning headache
Morning headache is one of the questions asked about disordered sleep, but snoring is the symptom named as the hallmark.
Trouble falling asleep at night
Insomnia is listed as another cause of disordered sleep; the hallmark of obstructive sleep apnea is loud, persistent snoring.

Correct, which matters because a loud snap can radiate to the apex and to the pulmonic area and be mistaken for P2.
By its variation with the respiratory cycle
Respiratory variation is what characterizes physiologic splitting of S2.
By being heard only with the bell
The opening snap is heard best with the diaphragm, not the bell, because it is high pitched.
By its low pitch and rumbling quality
Low pitch and rumbling describe the murmur of mitral stenosis that may follow, not the snap itself.

C.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
C.q: What happens to mitral valve prolapse on squatting or leg raise?
opts: It is moved later in systole
Correct, because the increased ventricular volume delays the point at which the redundant leaflet balloons into the atrium.
It disappears entirely
The described effect is a shift in timing rather than abolition.
It becomes louder and earlier
Increased filling moves it LATER in systole rather than earlier.
It becomes a diastolic murmur
The click and following murmur remain systolic; only their timing within systole shifts.

C.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
C.q: Why does squatting from standing make aortic stenosis louder?
opts: The outflow tract obstruction worsens
Increased filling REDUCES the obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is why that murmur softens.
The valve area decreases
The valve is unchanged; what changes is the volume of blood crossing it.
More blood rushes past the narrowed valve
Correct — squatting forces leg volume back to the heart, raising preload and left ventricular filling.
Intrathoracic pressure rises
That is the Valsalva mechanism.

C.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
C.q: Which is an older name for crackles?
opts: Stridor
Stridor is a continuous, high-pitched musical sound from upper airway narrowing, not another name for crackles.
Rales
Correct: crackles were formerly called rales, and the two words are still used for the same non-musical, discontinuous sound.
Wheezes
Wheezes are continuous MUSICAL sounds; crackles are non-musical and discontinuous.
Rhonchi
Rhonchi are a variant of wheezes, continuous and lower in pitch, not another name for crackles.

C.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
C.q: Which accompanying finding raises concern most in a patient with new petechiae?
opts: Lesions that do not itch
Itch is not a criterion. Mucosal bleeding or systemic illness raises the concern.
Mucosal bleeding
Correct. Concern increases with mucosal bleeding or systemic illness. Petechiae and purpura have possible causes in platelet or vascular disorders, medications and other conditions.
A history of recent sun exposure
Sun exposure is not on the list. Concern rises with mucosal bleeding or systemic illness.
Lesions on the lower legs
Distribution is recorded, but leg lesions alone are not the named concern. Mucosal bleeding or systemic illness is.

C.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
C.q: Which exposure is linked with possible B12 deficiency?
opts: Nitrous oxide
Correct. Nitrous oxide exposure is listed with possible B12 deficiency in the medication history, beside metformin and acid-suppressing medications.
Lead from pre-1978 buildings
Lead exposure (occupational, renovation, pre-1978 buildings) is a separate exposure question. Nitrous oxide is the one tied to B12 deficiency.
Benzene
Benzene is a marrow-toxic chemical, asked about for marrow damage. Nitrous oxide is the exposure tied to B12 deficiency.
Aspirin
Aspirin is asked about in the medication history beside anti-inflammatories and anticoagulants, but nitrous oxide is the exposure listed with possible B12 deficiency.

C.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
C.q: In whom is a physiologic S3 expected?
opts: Children and young adults to about 35 or 40
Correct, and in the last trimester of pregnancy. In adults over 40 the same sound is pathologic.
Only in patients with valve disease
A physiologic S3 occurs in healthy children, young adults and late pregnancy.
Adults over 40
In that group S3 is PATHOLOGIC, arising from high left ventricular filling pressures.
Trained athletes of any age
A normal S4 is described in trained athletes rather than a physiologic S3.

C.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
C.q: How do maneuvers affect the murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Increases with squatting; decreases with Valsalva
That is the aortic stenosis pattern; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy behaves oppositely.
Increases only with isometric handgrip
Handgrip is not listed as increasing this murmur; squatting decreases it, and Valsalva and standing increase it.
Unchanged by any maneuver
It does change: squatting decreases this murmur, and Valsalva and standing increase it.
Decreases on squatting, increases on Valsalva
Correct, and it is exactly the reverse of aortic stenosis — which is the point of doing the maneuvers at all. Standing increases it too.

C.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
C.q: An anemic patient's stool blood test is positive. What does the result establish?

Even a positive test leaves the cause of the anemia undetermined.
Neither source nor cause
Correct. A positive stool blood test leaves the source and the cause of the anemia undetermined; further evaluation follows the history, examination and type of anemia.
A colon cancer as the cause
A positive test names no lesion: source and cause remain undetermined.
The bleeding is from the stomach
A positive result does not locate the bleeding: the source stays undetermined, as does the cause of the anemia.

C.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
C.q: What produces crackles?
opts: Rapid airflow through nearly closed bronchi
Rapid airflow through bronchi narrowed almost to closure produces WHEEZES, which are continuous and musical.
Roughened pleural layers sliding together
Inflamed visceral and parietal pleura sliding against each other produce a pleural RUB, grating and biphasic.
Small airways snapping open on inspiration
Correct: crackles are non-musical, discontinuous sounds made when deflated small airways abruptly snap open during inspiration.
Airflow through a narrowed upper airway
Airflow through a narrowing in the upper respiratory tract produces STRIDOR, best heard over the neck on inspiration.

C.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
C.q: Which chest shape is shown?
opts: Thoracic kyphoscoliosis
Kyphoscoliosis is an abnormal spinal curvature with vertebral rotation that deforms the chest asymmetrically.
Funnel chest (pectus excavatum)
Funnel chest is a depression of the lower sternum, not an evenly rounded chest with a wide anteroposterior diameter.
Pigeon chest (pectus carinatum)
Pigeon chest has the sternum displaced forward with the adjacent costal cartilages depressed, a pointed rather than rounded profile.
Barrel chest
Correct: the cross-section is nearly round, with an increased anteroposterior diameter; normal in infancy, and it often accompanies aging and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

C.q: What causes a pulmonic ejection sound?
opts: Mitral valve prolapse
That produces a mid to late systolic click rather than an early ejection sound.
Pulmonary artery dilatation or hypertension
Correct, whereas an aortic ejection sound may accompany a dilated aorta or aortic valve disease from congenital stenosis or a bicuspid valve. Pulmonic stenosis also causes it.
Inflammation of the pericardium
That produces a scratchy friction rub heard through both systole and diastole.
Stenosis of the mitral valve
That produces an opening snap in very early diastole.

C.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
C.q: Which duration defines a chronic cough?
opts: More than 2 weeks
Two weeks is still acute; acute cough runs up to 3 weeks and chronic begins beyond 8 weeks.
More than 3 weeks
Beyond 3 weeks a cough is SUBACUTE; chronic begins only after 8 weeks.
More than 8 weeks
Correct: cough is acute under 3 weeks, subacute at 3-8 weeks and chronic beyond 8 weeks.
More than 12 weeks
The threshold is lower: a cough lasting more than 8 weeks is already chronic.

C.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
C.q: A patient with hypertension and a prior myocardial infarction has dyspnea that is worse lying flat, with paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema and weight gain. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Left-sided heart failure
Correct: left-sided heart failure can be gradual or sudden, worse with exertion or lying flat, with orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, edema and weight gain.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
This disease is slowly progressive exertional dyspnea after smoking or exposures; orthopnea, edema and weight gain point to the heart.
Asthma
Asthma is episodic wheezing, worse at night but with symptom-free intervals, and does not bring edema and weight gain.
Pneumonia
Pneumonia is acute with fever, chills, sputum and pleuritic pain, not edema and weight gain after a myocardial infarction.

C.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
C.q: Which motor finding may result from corticospinal tract involvement in B12 deficiency?
opts: Spasticity and hyperreflexia
Correct. Lateral corticospinal tract involvement may cause spasticity and hyperreflexia; peripheral neuropathy can coexist, so reflexes vary.
Flaccid weakness with fasciculations
That is not the listed corticospinal picture. Corticospinal involvement gives spasticity and hyperreflexia.
Resting tremor and rigidity
Those are not B12 findings here. Corticospinal involvement may cause spasticity and hyperreflexia.
Loss of vibration sense
Lost vibration sense comes from the POSTERIOR COLUMNS. The corticospinal tracts give spasticity and hyperreflexia.

C.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
C.q: How is Homan's sign elicited, and what is a positive result?
opts: Compression of both wrist arteries; delayed hand filling

Homan's sign is elicited at the ankle with the knee bent, so a wrist maneuver cannot be it. Compressing the radial and ulnar arteries, then releasing one and watching the hand fill, is the Allen test of arterial patency in the hand. The tell: Homan's sign looks for a clot in the leg veins, while this checks the arteries that supply the hand.
Quick ankle dorsiflexion, knee bent; pain behind it

Correct. The stem asks for both halves of the sign, and this option gives both: quickly and forcefully dorsiflex the foot at the ankle while keeping the knee bent, and a positive result is pain behind the knee during the maneuver. It is the test that checks for deep vein thrombosis, and a positive result has traditionally been thought of as a clinical sign of it.
Thumb pressure for two seconds; a persisting depression

Thumb pressure answers a different question: whether swelling pits, not whether a movement hurts. Pressing firmly with the thumb for at least 2 seconds and seeing a lasting depression is the test for pitting edema. The tell: Homan's sign puts no pressure on the skin; it is a forced ankle movement with the knee bent.
Simultaneous radial and femoral palpation; a delay

Simultaneous radial and femoral palpation compares the timing of two arterial pulses and says nothing about a vein. A lag between them is pulse lag, which should make you consider coarctation of the aorta. The tell: Homan's sign is a maneuver on the foot with pain as its result, while pulse lag is a palpation finding with a delay as its result.
C.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 114

C.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
C.q: After a recent procedure, a patient with emphysema has decreased tactile fremitus, hyperresonance and absent breath sounds on one side, and the trachea is midline. Which condition fits?
opts: Atelectasis
Atelectasis is dull with ipsilateral tracheal deviation, not hyperresonant.
Pleural effusion
An effusion also lowers fremitus and breath sounds, but it is DULL to percussion, not hyperresonant.
Pneumonia
Pneumonia is dull with INCREASED fremitus and bronchial breath sounds.
Pneumothorax
Correct: decreased or absent fremitus, a hyperresonant or tympanic note and decreased or absent breath sounds on one side are the pneumothorax findings; the trachea shifts only with tension.

C.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
C.q: Which words describe the quality of a murmur?
opts: Systolic, diastolic, continuous
Those describe timing.
Blowing, harsh, rumbling, musical
Correct, and quality is distinct from pitch, which is categorized simply as high, medium or low.
Crescendo, decrescendo, plateau
Those describe shape, the configuration of intensity over time.
High, medium, low
Those are the categories of pitch.

C.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
C.q: What happens when a patient stands quickly from squatting?
opts: Intrathoracic pressure rises

A rise in intrathoracic pressure is the Valsalva maneuver, forceful expiration against a closed airway as the supine patient bears down. Standing changes where the blood sits, not the pressure in the chest. The tell: both lower preload and make the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur louder, but only Valsalva strains against a closed airway.
Afterload rises through muscular contraction

Standing from a squat involves no sustained muscle squeeze; it acts on preload, as blood moves to the legs and venous return falls. A sustained squeeze is the isometric handgrip, which increases the murmurs of mitral regurgitation, mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation, among others. The tell: standing changes filling, not grip.
Blood returns from the legs and preload rises

Blood returning from the legs and preload rising describe the reverse move, squatting from standing or a leg raise, which forces stored blood back to the heart. Standing up does the opposite. The tell: on squatting the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur softens and the aortic stenosis murmur gets louder; on standing, the two swap.
Blood pools in the legs; preload falls

Correct. Standing quickly from a squat lets blood move to the legs, so less returns to the heart (decreased venous return) and left ventricular preload falls. With less filling, the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur becomes louder and the aortic stenosis murmur gets softer, which is how this maneuver separates the two.

C.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
C.q: Which palpation finding fits lobar pneumonia?
opts: Trachea pulled toward the lesion
Ipsilateral tracheal deviation is the atelectasis finding; in pneumonia the trachea stays midline.
Increased tactile fremitus
Correct: pneumonia increases tactile fremitus over the consolidation, with a unilateral decrease or delay in chest expansion.
Absent tactile fremitus
Decreased or absent fremitus fits pneumothorax and pleural effusion, where air or fluid separates lung from chest wall.
Trachea pushed to the other side
A trachea shifted toward the unaffected side fits a tension pneumothorax or a large effusion; in pneumonia it is midline.

D.q: Which is the most common respiratory problem after surgery?
opts: Atelectasis
Correct: atelectasis is the most common respiratory issue to occur after surgery.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax follows trauma or procedures, but it is not the most common postoperative respiratory problem.
Pulmonary embolism
Surgery is a risk factor for pulmonary embolism, but the most common postoperative respiratory problem is atelectasis.
Pneumonia
Pneumonia can follow surgery or aspiration, but atelectasis is named the most common postoperative respiratory problem.

D.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: What is Grey Turner sign, and what does it suggest?
opts: Spoon nails; iron deficiency
Spoon nails are koilonychia. Grey Turner sign is flank ecchymosis.
Periumbilical ecchymosis; internal bleeding
That describes Cullen sign. Grey Turner sign is flank ecchymosis.
Flank ecchymosis; internal bleeding
Correct. Grey Turner sign is flank ecchymosis from retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal bleeding; it is also possible in severe pancreatitis.
Flank pain; kidney stones
Grey Turner sign is not pain; it is flank ECCHYMOSIS from retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal bleeding.

D.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
D.q: Retraction of the lower intercostal spaces during inspiration occurs in which condition?
opts: Pleural effusion
A large pleural effusion causes ASYMMETRIC expansion, not inspiratory retraction of the intercostal spaces.
Severe asthma
Correct: retraction of the intercostal spaces on inspiration occurs in severe asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and upper airway obstruction.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax brings hyperresonance and decreased or absent breath sounds on one side; retractions are listed for asthma and obstruction.
Lobar pneumonia
Lobar pneumonia causes a unilateral decrease or delay in expansion with increased fremitus, not intercostal retraction.

D.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
D.q: Aspirated material most often enters the right bronchial tree. Which feature of the right main bronchus explains this?
opts: It is narrower
The right main bronchus is WIDER, not narrower, and more vertical, which is why aspirated material favors it.
It passes under the aortic arch
The LEFT main bronchus passes beneath the aortic arch before entering the left hilum; the right is the more vertical one.
It is longer
Length belongs to the LEFT main bronchus, which is longer and more horizontal; the right is shorter and more vertical.
It is more vertical
Correct: the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so aspirated material more commonly enters the right bronchial tree.

D.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
D.q: Over the right lower chest there is dullness, increased tactile fremitus, bronchial breath sounds and egophony, and the trachea is midline. Which condition fits?
opts: Pneumonia
Correct: pneumonia gives dullness over the airless area, increased fremitus, bronchial sounds, late inspiratory crackles and positive transmitted voice sounds, with a midline trachea.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is hyperresonant or tympanic with decreased or absent fremitus, not dull with increased fremitus.
Pleural effusion
An effusion is dull too, but it DECREASES fremitus and breath sounds over the fluid.
Atelectasis
Atelectasis is dull with DIMINISHED fremitus and pulls the trachea toward the affected side.

D.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
D.q: A patient with sudden dyspnea has a history of emphysema and a recent procedure, and reports abrupt pain on one side of the chest. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Pneumonia
Pneumonia is acute with fever, chills, cough and sputum after illness or aspiration, not abrupt one-sided pain after a procedure.
Pneumothorax
Correct: pneumothorax is sudden dyspnea with abrupt unilateral pleuritic pain, after trauma, a recent procedure, emphysema or a prior pneumothorax.
Asthma
Asthma is episodic wheezing with allergen and exercise triggers, not abrupt unilateral pain after a procedure.
Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is also sudden, but its history is prior clots, surgery, immobility, cancer, estrogen or pregnancy rather than emphysema.

D.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
D.q: Which percussion finding fits asthma?
opts: Resonant to diffusely hyperresonant
Correct: in asthma percussion is resonant to diffusely hyperresonant, over hyperinflated lungs.
Dull over the affected area
Dullness over an airless area is the pneumonia finding, where consolidation replaces air.
Dull over the fluid
Dullness over the fluid, with a high diaphragmatic level, is the pleural effusion finding.
Tympanic over one side
A hyperresonant or tympanic note over ONE side is the pneumothorax finding; asthma is diffuse.

D.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: Which sign is shown on this patient's side?
opts: Jaundice
Jaundice is a diffuse yellow color of the skin. These are purple bruises across the flank: Grey Turner sign.
Cullen sign
Cullen sign is around the umbilicus. Bruising of the flank is Grey Turner sign.
Petechiae
Petechiae are pinpoint spots. These are larger bruises across the flank.
Grey Turner sign
Correct. Bruising across the flank is Grey Turner sign: flank ecchymosis from retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal bleeding.

D.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
D.q: Sharp chest pain is worse lying supine and with inspiration, and improves when the patient sits forward. Which diagnosis does this suggest?
opts: Pleuritis
Pleuritis gives sharp pain with inspiration or cough, but relief on sitting forward is the positional pattern of pericarditis.
Costochondritis
Costochondritis is localized and reproducible by palpation; position and leaning forward are not what define it.
Pericarditis
Correct: sharp, positional pain that is worse supine or with inspiration and improved by sitting forward points to pericarditis.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease

D.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
D.q: Where do venous ulcers typically occur?
opts: Over the shins only
The shins are one of the sites tested for pitting, but venous ulcers occur around the ankles.
On the dorsum of the foot

Over the tips of the toes
Distal painful ulceration is more characteristic of arterial insufficiency.
Around the ankles, over both malleoli

D.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
D.q: On inspection, one side of the chest lags behind the other in respiratory movement. What does this suggest?
opts: Upper airway obstruction
Upper airway obstruction causes stridor and intercostal retraction, a problem affecting both sides rather than a one-sided lag.
Generalized hyperinflation from asthma
Hyperinflation affects both lungs evenly, giving generalized hyperresonance rather than a lag on one side.
Normal age-related change
Aging raises the anteroposterior diameter ratio but does not make one side lag; a unilateral lag points to pleural or phrenic disease.
Pleural disease or phrenic nerve injury

D.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
D.q: What position brings out aortic regurgitation?
opts: Standing quickly from a squat
That reduces preload and is used to distinguish hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from aortic stenosis.
Sitting forward, breath held after exhaling
Correct, and the same position is used for the pericardial friction rub — both are brought closer to the chest wall by it.
Left lateral decubitus with the bell
Left lateral decubitus with the bell is the position for mitral stenosis, S3 and S4.
Supine while bearing down
That is the Valsalva maneuver, used to distinguish hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

D.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
D.q: How is a patient asked to perform a Valsalva?
opts: Squat quickly from standing

Squatting from standing does the opposite of Valsalva: it forces blood from the legs back to the heart and raises preload, so the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur softens and the aortic stenosis murmur grows louder. The tell: squatting is a change in posture that adds filling; Valsalva is a strain while supine that lowers it.
Lean forward and exhale completely

Sitting up, leaning forward, exhaling completely and holding the breath is the position for bringing out aortic regurgitation and the friction rub, not the Valsalva. Valsalva is done with the patient supine, bearing down. The tell: this position helps you hear sounds, while Valsalva is a strain that decreases left ventricular filling.
Grip both hands tightly for thirty seconds

Gripping tightly is the isometric handgrip, a different maneuver that increases the murmurs of mitral regurgitation, pulmonic stenosis, ventricular septal defect, aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis. The tell: handgrip is a squeeze of the hands, while Valsalva is forceful expiration against a closed airway.
Bear down as if straining

Correct. Ask the supine patient to bear down as if straining during a bowel movement, or to push against your hand on the mid-abdomen. This forceful expiration against a closed airway raises intrathoracic pressure and decreases left ventricular filling, so a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur increases while an aortic stenosis murmur gets softer or does not change.

D.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: Which murmur may be heard in a patient with anemia?
opts: A continuous machinery murmur
A continuous murmur is not among the anemia findings. The possible murmur is a systolic flow murmur.
A systolic flow murmur
Correct. The hyperdynamic circulation of anemia can produce a systolic flow murmur, along with tachycardia, bounding pulses and a prominent precordial impulse.
A diastolic decrescendo murmur
Anemia's murmur is systolic, from flow through a hyperdynamic circulation, not a diastolic one.
An opening snap with a rumble
An opening snap and rumble are not anemia findings. The possible murmur is a systolic flow murmur.

Pleural effusion

Asthma

Lung cancer

D.q: What does this tongue show?
opts: Angular cheilitis
Angular cheilitis is at the mouth corners. The finding is the smooth, red tongue itself.
Palatal petechiae
Palatal petechiae are pinpoint red dots on the roof of the mouth. This is a diffusely red, smooth tongue.
Oral mucosal pallor
Pallor makes the mucosa pale. This tongue is beefy red: glossitis.
Glossitis
Correct. A smooth, glossy, beefy-red tongue is glossitis, inflammation of the tongue, which suggests possible iron, B12 or folate deficiency.
D.alt: A protruded tongue that is smooth, glossy and beefy red.

D.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
D.q: Which diagnosis belongs to the sharp, pleuritic chest pain pattern?
opts: Pneumothorax
Correct: sharp pain worse with inspiration or cough suggests pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia or pleuritis.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection is the sudden, tearing pattern: abrupt, maximal early and radiating to the back, rather than pleuritic.
Costochondritis
Costochondritis is the localized, reproducible pattern, provoked by movement or palpation with focal tenderness.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Reflux is the burning, postprandial pattern, worse after meals, bending over or lying down, with possible regurgitation.

D.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
D.q: How much weight can accumulate before pitting edema appears?
opts: About 10 percent of body weight
Correct, which is why the symptom can be well established before the sign is visible — and why daily morning weights are a useful thing to recommend.
About 1 percent of body weight
The figure given is ten times larger, at around 10 percent.
About 25 percent of body weight
The figure named is 10 percent rather than a quarter of body weight.
Any gain at all produces visible pitting
A substantial amount accumulates first — about 10 percent of body weight.

D.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
D.q: A patient with acute hemorrhage has a normal hemoglobin. What should be remembered?
opts: Instability can precede the fall in hemoglobin
Correct. In acute hemorrhage the patient may become unstable before the hemoglobin falls, so vital signs, mental status, perfusion and ongoing loss guide the response.
Transfusion should be given at once
Oxygen and transfusion are given according to the clinical situation, not routinely.
A normal hemoglobin excludes major bleeding
It does not: the hemoglobin may not have fallen yet. Instability can come first.
The bleeding is too small to matter
Hemoglobin lags in acute hemorrhage; judge by vital signs, mental status, perfusion and ongoing loss.

D.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: What is glossitis?
opts: Fissures at the corners of the mouth
Inflammation and fissures at the corners of the mouth are angular cheilitis. Glossitis is a smooth, sore, beefy-red tongue.
A smooth, sore, beefy-red tongue
Correct. Glossitis is inflammation of the tongue: smooth, sore and beefy red. It suggests possible iron, B12 or folate deficiency.
Red pinpoint dots on the palate
Those are palatal petechiae, mucosal bleeding. Glossitis is a smooth, sore, beefy-red tongue.
A pale, dry oral mucosa
A pale mucosa is pallor. Glossitis is a red, inflamed, smooth tongue.

D.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills when using the stethoscope diaphragm and bell with relation to specific heart sounds
D.q: How much pressure is used with each chest piece?
opts: The bell firmly, the diaphragm lightly
The pressures are the other way round: bell light, diaphragm firm.
Both firmly
The bell is applied lightly, since pressing it firmly stretches the skin and turns it into a diaphragm.
Both lightly
The diaphragm is pressed firmly; only the bell is applied lightly.
The bell lightly, the diaphragm firmly
Correct, and the bell must still make contact with no gaps — pressing it hard would stretch the skin and turn it into a diaphragm.

D.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
D.q: When is physiologic splitting of S2 audible?
opts: During inspiration
Correct — the two components are normally fused as one sound during expiration and audibly separate on inspiration. Hearing both on inspiration is normal.
During expiration
The components are normally FUSED during expiration and separate on inspiration.
Throughout the respiratory cycle
Splitting present throughout would not be the physiologic pattern, which varies with respiration.
Only when the patient holds their breath
The splitting is defined by its variation with the respiratory cycle rather than by breath holding.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 15

D.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: In clubbing, how does the phalangeal depth ratio change?
opts: The two depths shrink equally
Clubbing enlarges the nail-base depth; the ratio rises rather than staying even.
Depth at the end joint exceeds depth at the nail base
That is the NORMAL relationship. In clubbing the depth at the nail base is the greater.
The nail becomes thin and spoon-shaped
A thin, spoon-shaped nail is koilonychia, an iron clue. Clubbing makes the nail-base depth the greater.
Depth at the nail base exceeds depth at the end joint
Correct. The phalangeal depth ratio compares the distal phalangeal depth at the nail base with the interphalangeal depth; in clubbing the nail-base depth becomes the greater.

D.io: Compare and contrast the auscultatory findings of crackles, wheezes, and rhonchi
D.q: A high-pitched inspiratory whistling is heard over the neck without a stethoscope. What does it signal?
opts: Lower airway narrowing
Lower airway narrowing produces wheezes, expiratory or continuous, over the lung; stridor is upper airway obstruction.
Upper airway obstruction
Correct: high-pitched inspiratory whistling is stridor, from obstruction in the larynx or trachea, and it needs urgent evaluation and immediate intervention.
Inflamed pleural surfaces
Inflamed pleura give a grating pleural rub over the axilla and bases, not inspiratory whistling over the neck.
Secretions in large airways
Secretions give rhonchi, which may clear with coughing; whistling over the neck on inspiration is stridor.

D.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
D.q: Where is the right ventricular impulse felt?
opts: Second intercostal space at the right sternal border

The 2nd intercostal space at the right sternal border is the aortic auscultation area, where you listen to a valve, not where a ventricle is palpated. The right ventricular impulse is lower and on the left, in the 3rd to 5th left intercostal spaces. The tell: the right ventricle is felt to the LEFT of the sternum, not high on the right.
Over the carotid arteries

The carotid arteries are palpated in the neck for the pulse and to help time murmurs, not for a ventricular impulse. A systolic murmur coincides with the carotid upstroke, which is why you feel the carotid while listening. The tell: a ventricular impulse is felt on the chest wall, and the right one in the 3rd to 5th left intercostal spaces.
The 3rd to 5th left intercostal spaces

Correct. The right ventricular impulse is felt in the 3rd, 4th and 5th left intercostal spaces, and with pressure overload it may extend to the subxiphoid process. With volume overload, as in atrial septal defect, it lies along the left sternal border toward the left cardiac border; unlike the left ventricular impulse, its diameter is not useful.
Fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line

The 5th intercostal space at or just medial to the left midclavicular line is the normal spot for the point of maximal impulse, the LEFT ventricular apex, which marks the heart's left border. The tell: the midclavicular line means the left ventricle, while the right ventricular impulse is felt in the 3rd to 5th left intercostal spaces.
