D.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
D.q: Which condition causes a unilateral decrease or delay in chest expansion?
opts: Asthma
Asthma reduces expansion on BOTH sides, with symmetric hyperresonance and wheezes, rather than on one side.
Paralysis of one hemidiaphragm
Correct: a unilateral decrease or delay occurs in chronic fibrosis, pleural effusion, lobar pneumonia, pleural pain with splinting, unilateral bronchial obstruction and hemidiaphragm paralysis.
Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation is episodic air hunger and sighing, not a structural cause of one-sided reduced expansion.
Chronic bronchitis
Chronic bronchitis is a productive cough with progressive dyspnea; it is not on the list for unilateral decreased expansion.

D.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: Once a patient reports bleeding, which four features of it should be defined?
opts: Color, smell, temperature and texture
Appearance helps name the bleeding (melena against hematochezia), but the history defines onset, frequency, amount and duration.
Triggers, family pattern, cost and treatment
Family patterns belong to the family history, not the description of one bleed. Define onset, frequency, amount and duration.
Onset, frequency, amount and duration
Correct. For any bleeding, define its onset, frequency, amount and duration; for menstrual bleeding also flooding, protection changes and daily impact.
Location, radiation, timing and relief
Those are pain descriptors. Bleeding is characterized by onset, frequency, amount and duration.

D.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
D.q: Clubbing is associated with which lung condition?
opts: Atelectasis
Atelectasis is collapsed lung, common after surgery, and is not among the diseases associated with clubbing.
Pneumothorax
Pneumothorax is a sudden event with hyperresonance and absent sounds; it is not associated with clubbing.
Asthma
Asthma is episodic wheezing and chest tightness and is not on the clubbing list, which includes interstitial lung disease.
Interstitial lung disease
Correct: clubbing is seen in interstitial lung disease and pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, lung abscess, lung cancer and congenital heart disease.

D.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: Which cause of anemia works by IMPAIRED red cell production?
opts: Renal failure
Correct. Impaired production covers iron, B12 and folic acid deficiency, renal failure, chronic disease and hematologic neoplasm or metastatic disease.
Sickle cell disease
Sickle cell disease causes anemia by destruction: it is an intrinsic hemolytic anemia. Impaired production includes renal failure, chronic disease and nutrient deficiency.
Transfusion reaction
A transfusion reaction is extrinsic hemolysis, destruction of red cells. Impaired production instead includes renal failure, chronic disease and marrow neoplasm or metastasis.
Heavy menstrual bleeding
Menstrual bleeding is a blood loss cause, alongside trauma and gastrointestinal loss. Impaired production includes renal failure, chronic disease and iron, B12 or folate deficiency.

D.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
D.q: Over normal air-filled lung, how do the patient's whispered words come through?
opts: Faint and indistinct, if heard at all
Correct: over normal lung whispered words are faint and indistinct, if heard at all; over consolidated lung they are louder and clearer.
Muffled but louder than speech
Over normal lung both spoken and whispered words are muffled and indistinct; a whisper is fainter, not louder.
Changed from "ee" to "ay"
"Ee" heard as "ay" is egophony, a sign of consolidation, and uses the spoken voice rather than a whisper.
Louder and clearer than expected
Louder, clearer whispered sounds are POSITIVE whispered pectoriloquy, a sign of consolidation.

D.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
D.q: Which is assessed when an anemic patient may be in a bleeding emergency?
opts: Vital signs, mental status, perfusion
Correct. In the emergency assess vital signs, mental status, skin perfusion and ongoing blood loss, then escalate.
Nail shape, hair shedding and diet
These are not what the emergency assessment checks. Assess vital signs, mental status, skin perfusion and ongoing blood loss.
Family history and ancestry
Family history is not what the emergency assessment checks. Assess vital signs, mental status, skin perfusion and ongoing blood loss.
Romberg test and gait
The neurologic examination belongs to the B12 work-up. The emergency calls for vital signs, mental status, perfusion and ongoing loss.

D.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
D.q: Which muscles contract during INSPIRATION when accessory muscles are being used?
opts: Pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi
Those two muscles border the triangle of safety for chest tubes; the inspiratory accessory muscles are the sternocleidomastoid and scalene.
Scalenes and abdominal obliques
The abdominal obliques work in expiration; inspiration recruits the sternocleidomastoid together with the scalenes.
Sternocleidomastoid and scalenes
Correct: the sternocleidomastoid and scalene contract during inspiration; the intercostals and abdominal obliques contract during expiration.
Intercostals and abdominal obliques
Those contract during EXPIRATION; the inspiratory accessory muscles are the sternocleidomastoid and scalene.

D.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: What does the pulled-down lower eyelid in this picture show?
opts: Scleral icterus
Icterus is yellowing of the sclera, the white of the eye. Here the lid's lining is pale: pallor.
Conjunctival pallor
Correct. The inner lining of the lower lid, the palpebral conjunctiva, is pale: conjunctival pallor, one of the sites where the pallor of anemia is looked for.
Normal conjunctiva
This lining is not a normal finding here: it is pale, which is conjunctival pallor, one of the listed sites for the pallor of anemia.
Palatal petechiae
Palatal petechiae are red dots on the roof of the mouth. This is a pale eyelid lining.
D.alt: A lower eyelid pulled down to show a pale, almost white inner lining.

D.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
D.q: Where does the murmur of pulmonic stenosis radiate?
opts: To the left axilla

Pulmonic stenosis does not radiate out to the left axilla; when loud, it spreads from the pulmonic area toward the left shoulder and neck. The other midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur here, aortic stenosis, goes to the carotids and down the left sternal border. The tell: the axilla is out to the side, while pulmonic stenosis travels upward.
Toward the left shoulder and neck, if loud

Correct. Pulmonic stenosis is a midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, medium-pitched harsh murmur heard at the pulmonic area, and when it is loud it radiates toward the left shoulder and neck. The 'if loud' qualifier matters: a loud pulmonic stenosis murmur also brings a thrill, and no maneuvers are listed for it.
To the right sternum and xiphoid

That pattern belongs to tricuspid regurgitation, which spreads to the right sternum, the xiphoid and the left midclavicular line but NOT the axilla. It is a pansystolic, blowing, plateau murmur at the lower left sternal border. The tell: pulmonic stenosis sits high at the pulmonic area and radiates up toward the left shoulder and neck.
To the carotids and down the left sternal border

That spread belongs to aortic stenosis, the other midsystolic, crescendo-decrescendo, harsh murmur, which often radiates to the carotids, down the left sternal border and even to the apex. The tell: aortic stenosis goes to the carotids from the aortic area, while pulmonic stenosis goes toward the left shoulder and neck, and only when loud.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 68

D.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
D.q: Which structure forms the posterior border of the triangle of safety?
opts: The scapular line
The scapular line is a posterior vertical reference line on the back, not a border of the triangle, which lies in the midaxillary line.
Lateral border of the pectoralis major
The pectoralis major forms the ANTERIOR border of the triangle; the posterior border is the lateral edge of the latissimus dorsi.
The nipple line
The nipple line, at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, is the INFERIOR boundary; the posterior border is the latissimus dorsi.
Lateral border of the latissimus dorsi
Correct: the triangle is bounded by the latissimus dorsi posteriorly, the pectoralis major anteriorly and the nipple line (4th or 5th intercostal space) below.

D.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: Which cardiovascular finding is expected in a patient with significant anemia?
opts: A pericardial friction rub
A friction rub is not among the anemia findings. Expect tachycardia, a hyperdynamic circulation and possibly a systolic flow murmur.
Tachycardia with a hyperdynamic circulation
Correct. Anemia drives tachycardia and a hyperdynamic circulation, with possible bounding pulses, a prominent precordial impulse and a systolic flow murmur.
Bradycardia with weak, thready pulses
That reverses the picture. Anemia speeds the heart and makes the circulation hyperdynamic, with possible bounding pulses.
A loud diastolic rumble at the apex
The murmur anemia may cause is a SYSTOLIC flow murmur, not a diastolic rumble.

D.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
D.q: How should the respiratory history begin?
opts: With an open-ended question
Correct: begin with an open-ended question and let the patient describe the symptoms in their own words, then clarify onset, timing and triggers.
With a checklist of yes-or-no questions
Closed questions clarify details afterward; the opening is an open-ended question in the patient's own words.
With the functional severity questions
Walking distance and flights of stairs grade severity once the symptom is described; they do not open the history.
With the exposure history
The exposure history (tobacco, marijuana, recreational drugs, occupation, travel) is detailed later rather than used as the opening.

D.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills for maneuvers to evaluate murmurs
D.q: What does the Valsalva maneuver do hemodynamically?
opts: Raises preload by returning blood from the legs
That is squatting or leg raise, which increases venous return.
Increases afterload by sustained muscle contraction
That is the isometric handgrip.
Raises intrathoracic pressure, drops preload
Correct — forceful expiration against a closed airway, decreasing left ventricular filling. The hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur increases; aortic stenosis softens or does not change.
Has no effect on ventricular filling
The Valsalva specifically decreases left ventricular filling by raising intrathoracic pressure.

D.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying cardiac disorders
D.q: How is dyspnea defined?
opts: Sudden breathlessness waking the patient from sleep

Sudden breathlessness that wakes the patient is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, usually about 1 to 2 hours after going to bed and prompting the patient to sit up, stand up or go to a window for air. It is one particular pattern, not the definition of dyspnea. The tell: it is tied to sleep, while dyspnea is defined against the level of exertion.
An unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat

An unpleasant awareness of the heartbeat defines palpitations, described as skipping, racing, fluttering or pounding, not dyspnea. Dyspnea is about breathing, not the heartbeat. The tell: palpitations may come with anxiety or hyperthyroidism and prompt an electrocardiogram, while dyspnea is judged against the level of exertion.
Awareness of breathing out of proportion to exertion

Correct. Dyspnea is an uncomfortable awareness of breathing that is inappropriate to a given level of exertion; that qualifier, out of proportion to exertion, separates it from ordinary breathlessness after effort. It is common in both cardiac and pulmonary problems, and orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea are its positional and night-time patterns.
Breathlessness that occurs only when supine

Breathlessness that comes on when lying supine and improves on sitting up is orthopnea, a specific type of dyspnea quantified by the number of pillows used for sleep. Dyspnea itself is defined by exertion, not position. The tell: 'only when supine' names a trigger, while dyspnea is defined by a mismatch with the level of exertion.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 7

D.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills when using the stethoscope diaphragm and bell with relation to specific heart sounds
D.q: Which sounds is the diaphragm better for?
opts: Bruits over peripheral arteries only
Bruits are auscultated in the peripheral vascular examination, but the diaphragm's cardiac role is the high-pitched sounds.
Only sounds at the apex
The diaphragm is used throughout the precordium rather than at one site.
S1, S2 and rubs
Correct — the high-pitched sounds. It is pressed firmly and used to listen throughout the precordium. The regurgitant murmurs too.
S3, S4 and mitral stenosis
Those are low-pitched and are better heard with the bell applied lightly.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 30

D.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: Which bleeding finding is looked for inside the mouth?
opts: Cullen sign
Cullen sign is periumbilical ecchymosis on the abdomen. In the mouth, look for palatal petechiae.
Palatal petechiae
Correct. The oral examination looks for palatal petechiae and other mucosal bleeding, beside pallor of the oral mucosa.
Koilonychia
Koilonychia is a nail finding. In the mouth, look for palatal petechiae and other mucosal bleeding.
Scleral icterus
Icterus is an eye finding. Inside the mouth the bleeding sign is palatal petechiae.

D.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
D.q: What can the murmur of aortic regurgitation be mistaken for?
opts: S3
S3 is a low-pitched early diastolic sound best heard with the bell.
An opening snap
An opening snap is a discrete high-pitched sound rather than a sustained blowing murmur.
Breath sounds
Correct, because it is high frequency and blowing. It is early diastolic, decrescendo, grade 1 to 3, from the aortic area down the left intercostal space.
A pericardial friction rub
A rub is scratchy and scraping, heard intermittently through both systole and diastole.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 77

D.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
D.q: What is the cardiac cycle?
opts: The period of ventricular contraction only

The period of ventricular contraction is systole, one of the two phases of the cycle, not the cycle itself. In systole, ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure and closes the mitral and tricuspid valves, producing S1. The tell: the word 'only' leaves out diastole, and the cycle is defined by both phases alternating.
The period of ventricular relaxation only

The period of ventricular relaxation and filling is diastole, the other phase, so it too is only part of the cycle. The full cycle alternates contraction and relaxation from the start of one heartbeat to the next. The tell: this mirrors the systole option; whichever single phase is named, the cycle needs both systole and diastole.
The interval between S1 and S2

The interval between S1 and S2 is systole, the period of ventricular contraction, which is only one of the cycle's two phases. The cardiac cycle runs from the start of one heartbeat to the beginning of the next and includes diastole as well. The tell: S1 to S2 covers systole only; S2 back to S1 is diastole, and the cycle needs both.
From the start of one heartbeat to the next

Correct. The cardiac cycle is the period between the start of one heartbeat and the beginning of the next, made of alternating periods of contraction and relaxation. It is divided into two phases, systole (ventricular contraction) and diastole (ventricular relaxation and filling), so an option naming only one phase describes part of the cycle, not the whole.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 12

D.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
D.q: In which type of atelectasis may fremitus be increased and adjacent tracheal sounds be transmitted?
opts: Left upper lobe atelectasis
The exception named is on the RIGHT, in the upper lobe next to the trachea; the left upper lobe is not singled out.
Left lower lobe atelectasis
Left lower lobe atelectasis follows the usual rule: diminished fremitus and absent sounds while the plug persists.
Right upper lobe atelectasis
Correct: atelectasis usually diminishes fremitus and abolishes breath sounds, except in right upper lobe atelectasis, where fremitus may be increased and adjacent tracheal sounds transmitted.
Right lower lobe atelectasis
The exception is the right UPPER lobe, beside the trachea; lower lobe atelectasis follows the usual pattern of diminished fremitus.

D.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
D.q: What is true of the ulnar pulse?
opts: It is always easily palpable
The normal ulnar pulse may not be palpable at all, so absence does not imply disease.
It is found at the lateral wrist
The lateral portion of the wrist carries the radial pulse; the ulnar is medial.
It is assessed with the wrist fully extended
Partially FLEXING the wrist may help find it, since it is palpated deeply on the flexor surface.
It may not be palpable even when normal
Correct — palpate deeply on the medial flexor surface of the wrist, and partially flexing the wrist may help find it.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 100

D.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
D.q: What are the skin findings of chronic arterial insufficiency?
opts: Thickened skin with brown pigmentation and pitting edema

Thickened skin, brown hemosiderin pigmentation and pitting edema are the findings of chronic VENOUS insufficiency, the other cause of chronic skin changes in the legs. Arterial insufficiency gives thin skin and no edema. The tell: thick, brown, swollen skin is venous; thin, shiny, hairless, cool skin is arterial.
Normal temperature with cyanosis when dependent

Normal temperature and cyanosis of the foot when dependent belong to chronic venous insufficiency, which also keeps normal pulses. Arterial insufficiency makes the skin cool to touch, and its color changes are pallor on elevation and dusky rubor. The tell: 'normal temperature' rules out the arterial picture, which is cool.
Thin shiny skin, hair loss, cool to touch

Correct. Thin, shiny skin, loss of hair and skin that is cool to touch are the skin findings of chronic arterial insufficiency. The color is pale or dusky red, and the rest of the picture fits: no edema, decreased pulses, foot pallor on elevation, dusky rubor, painful ulceration unless neuropathy is present, and gangrene.
Warm erythematous skin with bounding pulses

Warm, red skin with bounding pulses is the opposite of arterial insufficiency, which makes the skin cool to touch and the pulses decreased. Bounding is the top of the pulse amplitude scale (4+), not a sign of reduced arterial supply. The tell: insufficiency means less arterial flow, so expect cool skin and weak pulses.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 91

D.io: Define the physical examination findings of peripheral edema
D.q: How is pitting edema tested for?
opts: Dorsiflex the foot at the ankle with the knee bent

Quickly dorsiflexing the foot with the knee bent is Homan's sign, which checks for deep vein thrombosis by looking for pain behind the knee. It tests for pain, not for fluid in the tissues. The tell: pitting edema needs pressure on the skin and a lasting dent, while Homan's sign needs a joint movement and a pain response.
Press on the nail bed and time the refill

Pressing on the fingernails and timing how long the nail beds take to turn pink is capillary refill, which checks the nail bed rather than testing for edema. The tell: capillary refill watches color return in the nail bed, while pitting edema looks for a depression left in swollen skin over the foot, the ankle and the shins.
Press firmly with the thumb, two seconds

Correct. Press firmly with the thumb for at least 2 seconds over the dorsum of the foot, behind the medial malleolus and over the shins; pitting is the depression the thumb leaves. Its depth and how long it lasts set the grade, from 1+ (2 millimeters, disappearing rapidly) to 4+ (8 millimeters, lasting more than 2 minutes).
Press with the balls of the hand against the limb

Pressing the balls of the hand against the chest wall is how you feel a thrill, the vibration of a loud murmur, not how you test for edema. Pitting edema needs the focused pressure of a thumb held for at least 2 seconds. The tell: the flat of the hand senses vibration over the heart, while the thumb leaves a pit in swollen skin.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 88

D.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
D.q: Where is the brachial pulse found?
opts: Lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow

This has the right landmark on the wrong side: the brachial pulse lies MEDIAL to the biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa, not lateral to it. Lateral is the side that belongs to the radial pulse, but at the wrist rather than the elbow. The tell: brachial is medial at the elbow; radial is lateral at the wrist.
At the lateral portion of the wrist

The lateral portion of the wrist is where the radial pulse is felt, not the brachial. The brachial pulse is higher up the arm, at the elbow, medial to the biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa. The tell: the wrist pulses are radial (lateral) and ulnar (medial), while the brachial pulse is the one at the elbow.
Behind the medial malleolus

Behind the medial malleolus is the posterior tibial pulse, a site at the ankle, while the brachial pulse is in the arm, medial to the biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa. The tell: a malleolus means the ankle, so this names a foot pulse; the other foot pulse is the dorsalis pedis, on the dorsum lateral to the extensor tendon of the great toe.
Medial to the biceps tendon at the elbow

Correct. The brachial pulse is felt medial to the biceps tendon at the antecubital fossa, which is the landmark the stem is asking for. Palpating on the medial side of the tendon, not lateral to it, is the detail that finds the artery. Farther down the same limb, the radial pulse is at the lateral portion of the wrist and the ulnar pulse at the medial portion.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 98

D.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: Which is an example of an INTRINSIC (intracorpuscular) cause of hemolytic anemia?
opts: Sickle cell disease
Correct. Intrinsic, intracorpuscular causes lie in the red cell itself: sickle cell disease, the thalassemia syndromes, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and other hemoglobinopathies.
Transfusion reaction
A transfusion reaction destroys red cells from outside them, an extrinsic (extracorpuscular) cause. Intrinsic examples are defects of the cell itself, such as sickle cell disease.
Renal failure
Renal failure causes anemia by impaired red cell production, not hemolysis. Intrinsic hemolytic causes include sickle cell disease and the thalassemias.
Malaria
Malaria is an extrinsic cause of hemolysis, along with lupus and transfusion reactions. An intrinsic cause is a defect within the red cell, such as sickle cell disease.

D.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
D.q: Cough is a reflex response to irritation of receptors in which structures?
opts: Larynx, trachea or large bronchi
Correct: mucus, pus, blood, allergens, dust, foreign bodies or very hot or cold air irritate receptors in the larynx, trachea or large bronchi.
Alveoli and small bronchioles
The alveoli are the gas-exchange surface; the cough receptors sit in the larynx, trachea and large bronchi.
Visceral pleura
The visceral pleura lacks sensory nerves; cough receptors are in the larynx, trachea and large bronchi.
Parietal pleura and diaphragm
Irritation of the parietal pleura produces pleuritic pain; cough is triggered from the larynx, trachea and large bronchi.

D.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
D.q: Which auscultatory findings fit asthma?
opts: Bronchial sounds with egophony
Bronchial sounds with egophony over an involved area are the pneumonia (consolidation) findings.
Wheezes and a prolonged expiratory phase
Correct: asthma gives wheezes, possibly crackles, and a prolonged expiratory phase.
Absent sounds over a bronchial plug
Absent sounds while a bronchial plug persists are the atelectasis finding.
Absent breath sounds with a pleural rub
Decreased or absent sounds with a possible pleural rub are the pneumothorax or effusion findings.

D.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: A woman has progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, heavier menstrual bleeding and frequent ibuprofen use. Which history best addresses the SOURCE of her anemia?
opts: Travel destinations and febrile illness
Travel and fever look for infection; this history points to blood loss from the uterus or gastrointestinal tract.
Paresthesias and walking in the dark
Those are B12 neurologic clues. Her history points to menstrual and possible gastrointestinal blood loss.
Menstrual flooding and any melena
Correct. Heavier menstrual bleeding and frequent ibuprofen both point to blood loss: define menstrual flooding and protection changes, and ask about gastrointestinal bleeding such as melena.
Relatives needing a splenectomy
That is the hemolysis family history. Her clues point to blood loss.

D.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
D.q: What causes an opening snap?
opts: Rapid ventricular filling against a compliant ventricle

Rapid ventricular filling is S3 territory: S3 arises at the end of the rapid filling phase and is physiologic in children, young adults and late pregnancy. It is low-pitched, heard with the bell, with no stenotic valve involved. The tell: the opening snap is high-pitched, heard best with the diaphragm, and needs a stenotic mitral valve.
Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves

Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves produces S2, a normal heart sound at the start of diastole. The opening snap follows S2 and can be mistaken for its pulmonic component when it radiates to the pulmonic area. The tell: S2 is valves closing, while the snap is a stenotic mitral valve opening, with a high pitch and an obvious snap.
Abrupt deceleration as a stenotic mitral valve opens

Correct. An opening snap is a very early diastolic sound caused by abrupt deceleration as a STENOTIC mitral valve opens. It is high-pitched, heard best with the diaphragm just medial to the apex and along the lower left sternal border, and the obvious snap helps tell it from S2; as the leaflets calcify over time it becomes less audible.
Ballooning of the mitral valve into the left atrium

Ballooning of part of the mitral valve into the left atrium is mitral valve prolapse, which gives a mid to late SYSTOLIC click, often followed by a late systolic murmur. The opening snap is diastolic. The tell: prolapse is a redundant valve clicking in systole, while the snap is a stenotic valve opening early in diastole.
D.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 44

D.io: Identify disease processes that may be associated with clubbing and hemoptysis
D.q: Which non-pulmonary condition is associated with clubbing?
opts: Hypertension
Hypertension is relevant history for left-sided heart failure, not a cause of clubbing.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Reflux is a cause of burning chest pain and of cough, not of clubbing; inflammatory bowel disease is the bowel condition linked to it.
Inflammatory bowel disease
Correct: beyond the lung diseases, clubbing is seen in inflammatory bowel disease, congenital heart disease and malignancy.
Nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome is a transudative cause of pleural effusion, not a disease associated with clubbing.

D.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
D.q: In a patient with fever and cough, which pair of findings more than triples the likelihood of pneumonia?
opts: Bronchial breath sounds and egophony
Correct: with fever and cough, bronchial breath sounds plus egophony more than triples the likelihood of pneumonia.
Wheezes and prolonged expiration
Wheezes with a prolonged expiratory phase are the asthma findings, not the consolidation pair.
Vesicular sounds and resonance
Vesicular sounds and a resonant note are the NORMAL findings over air-filled lung.
Hyperresonance and absent fremitus
Hyperresonance with decreased or absent fremitus is the pneumothorax pattern, the opposite of consolidation.

D.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: Which belongs to the focused physical examination of an anemic patient?
opts: Visual acuity and visual fields
Eye charts are not part of it; the eye examination looks at the conjunctivae for pallor and the sclerae for icterus. The abdomen with liver and spleen is included.
Otoscopy of both ears
The ears are not on the focused list. It covers skin, conjunctivae, mouth, nails, nodes, heart, lungs, abdomen and a targeted neurologic examination.
Range of motion of the joints
A joint survey is not part of it. The abdomen, including liver and spleen, is.
Abdomen, liver and spleen

Correct. The focused examination covers general appearance and vital signs, skin, conjunctivae, mouth and nails, lymph nodes, heart and lungs, the abdomen with liver and spleen, and a targeted neurologic examination.

D.io: Describe the character of the apical impulse with reference to anatomy and ventricular function
D.q: Which conditions cause a right ventricular pressure overload impulse?
opts: Pulmonic stenosis and pulmonary hypertension
Correct, producing a more forceful tapping with a sustained duration — the right-sided mirror of aortic stenosis and hypertension on the left.
Aortic stenosis and hypertension
Those are the LEFT ventricular pressure overload examples.
Anxiety and hyperthyroidism
Those produce the hyperkinetic pattern on either side.
Atrial septal defect
That is the right ventricular VOLUME overload example, giving a slightly to markedly more forceful impulse.

D.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
D.q: How is the murmur of mitral stenosis best heard?
opts: With the diaphragm at the base, sitting forward
That approach suits aortic regurgitation and the pericardial friction rub.
Bell at the apex, left lateral decubitus
Correct — a low-pitched decrescendo rumble, mid to late diastolic, grade 1 to 4, with little or no radiation.
With the diaphragm at the apex, supine
The diaphragm at the apex is used for S1; a low-pitched rumble needs the bell.
With the bell in the aortic area
The aortic area carries aortic stenosis and the aortic ejection sound.

D.io: List presenting signs and symptoms from other organ systems associated with disorders of the hematological system.
D.q: Which nail-fold profile angle indicates clubbing?
opts: Less than 180 degrees
Under 180 degrees is the NORMAL angle. Clubbing pushes it past 180 degrees.
Greater than 180 degrees
Correct. A nail-fold profile angle under 180 degrees is normal; over 180 degrees indicates clubbing.
Exactly 90 degrees
A right angle is not the cut-off. Normal is under 180 degrees; clubbing is over 180 degrees.
Less than 160 degrees
An angle well under 180 degrees is normal. Clubbing is an angle greater than 180 degrees.

D.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
D.q: Which palpation findings are common over a fractured rib?
opts: A draining sinus tract
Sinus tracts are blind, inflammatory tracts opening onto the skin that suggest infection of the pleura and lung (tuberculosis, actinomycosis).
Tenderness, bruising and a bony step-off
Correct: tenderness, bruising and bony step-offs are common over fractured ribs; crepitus may also be felt in overt fractures.
Increased tactile fremitus
Increased fremitus reflects consolidated lung beneath, as in unilateral pneumonia, not a broken rib.
Crepitus with chest wall edema
Crepitus may be felt in overt fractures, but crepitus WITH chest wall edema is the mediastinitis pairing; the common fracture findings are tenderness, bruising and step-offs.

E.io: Demonstrate the proper clinical skills when using the stethoscope diaphragm and bell with relation to specific heart sounds
E.q: Which sounds is the bell better for?
opts: High-pitched sounds
The diaphragm is better for those — S1, S2, pericardial friction rubs, and the murmurs of aortic and mitral regurgitation.
Only murmurs, not heart sounds
The bell picks up S3 and S4 as well as the low-pitched murmur of mitral stenosis.
Low-pitched sounds
Correct — S3, S4 and the murmur of mitral stenosis. It is applied lightly to the skin, ensuring no gaps, at the apex and moving medially along the lower sternal border.
Both equally
The two chest pieces are specifically suited to different pitches.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 30

E.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
E.q: Where does the trachea bifurcate at the carina?
opts: Near the xiphoid process; T10 behind
T10 is the posterior inferior border of the lung; the carina is far higher, near the sternal angle and T4-T5.
Near the 6th rib; T7-T8 behind
T7-T8 is the posterior thoracentesis level; the trachea divides near the sternal angle at T4-T5.
Near the suprasternal notch; C7 behind
The suprasternal notch and C7 are higher landmarks; the carina sits lower, near the sternal angle and T4-T5.
Near the sternal angle; T4-T5 behind
Correct: the carina lies near the sternal angle anteriorly and at the T4-T5 level posteriorly.

E.io: Describe the elements related to interviewing and eliciting a medical history that aid in identifying pulmonary disorders
E.q: Which item belongs to the detailed exposure history?
opts: Flights of stairs climbed
Flights of stairs measure the functional severity of dyspnea; the exposure history covers substances, occupation and travel.
Recent travel
Correct: the exposure history covers tobacco and nicotine, marijuana (smoked, vaped or ingested), recreational drugs, occupational and environmental exposures, and recent travel.
Sputum color
Sputum color belongs to characterizing a productive cough (amount, color, consistency, odor, blood), not to the exposure history.
Morning headaches
Morning headache is one of the sleep questions asked about snoring and disordered sleep, not part of the exposure history.

E.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
E.q: What does the Allen test evaluate?
opts: Presence of deep vein thrombosis

Deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a leg vein, checked by Homan's sign (pain behind the knee on forced dorsiflexion of the foot), not by a hand test. The Allen test looks at arteries, not veins. The tell: the Allen test is done at the wrist and hand, while deep vein thrombosis is sought with a maneuver at the ankle.
The adequacy of capillary refill

Capillary refill is a separate check: press on the fingernails and time how long the nail beds take to turn pink. The Allen test compresses and releases named arteries at the wrist instead. The tell: capillary refill watches the nail bed as a whole, while the Allen test asks whether the radial and ulnar arteries are each patent.
Patency of the radial and ulnar arteries

Correct. The Allen test evaluates the arterial supply of the hand by assessing the patency of the radial and ulnar arteries. Compress both, have the patient clench the fist for 30 seconds, open it, then release the ulnar artery and watch the hand fill; repeat, releasing the radial, to check that artery.
The ratio of ankle to brachial pressure

The ratio of ankle to brachial systolic pressure is the ankle brachial index, calculated separately for each leg with a blood pressure cuff. It assesses the legs, while the Allen test assesses the hand. The tell: the index is a number worked out from pressures, while the Allen test is a bedside look at how the hand refills.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 108

E.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused cardiovascular physical examination
E.q: How long is the patient asked to clench the fist in the Allen test?
opts: Thirty seconds
Correct, with both arteries occluded. The fist is then opened and one artery released to watch the hand fill.
Two seconds
Two seconds is the minimum thumb pressure for testing pitting edema.
Ten minutes
Ten minutes supine is the rest period before measuring brachial pressure for an ankle brachial index.
Until the patient reports pain
The duration given is thirty seconds of clenching rather than being guided by symptoms.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 108

E.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
E.q: What causes a pericardial friction rub?
opts: Regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve

Regurgitant flow across an incompetent valve produces a regurgitant murmur, such as mitral or tricuspid regurgitation, and is one of the named causes of a murmur. A rub has no valvular cause; it comes from an inflamed pericardial sac. The tell: a regurgitant murmur is a 'swoosh' of blood flow, while the rub is a scratchy, scraping noise.
Reduced ventricular compliance

Reduced ventricular compliance, from hypertrophy or fibrosis, produces S4, a dull, low-pitched atrial gallop just before S1, heard with the bell. A friction rub is a pericardial sound, not a filling sound. The tell: the rub is high-pitched, best with the diaphragm, and scratchy through both systole and diastole.
Inflammation of the pericardial sac

Correct. A pericardial friction rub comes from inflammation of the pericardial sac, that is, pericarditis. It is a scratchy, scraping noise heard intermittently through both diastole and systole, high-pitched and best heard with the diaphragm, most often at Erb's point, and it may increase when the patient leans forward, exhales and holds the breath.
Turbulent flow across a stenotic valve

Turbulent flow across a stenotic valve produces a stenotic murmur, such as the low-pitched diastolic rumble of mitral or tricuspid stenosis, not a rub. The friction rub involves no valve; it comes from the inflamed pericardium. The tell: a stenotic murmur sits in one phase, while the rub scrapes through systole and diastole.

E.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
E.q: When egophony is present, how does the patient's spoken "ee" sound through the stethoscope?
opts: Like a louder "ninety-nine"
A louder "ninety-nine" is a positive BRONCHOPHONY result; egophony uses "ee".
Like "a"
Correct: with egophony the spoken "ee" sounds like "a" (or "ay"); over normal lung it is heard as a muffled long E.
Like a muffled long "ee"
A muffled long E is what you hear when egophony is NOT present, over normal air-filled lung.
Like a clear whisper
Louder, clearer whispered sounds are positive whispered pectoriloquy, a different test.

E.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
E.q: Which lesions cover the leg in this picture?
opts: Koilonychia
Koilonychia is a spoon-shaped nail, not a skin lesion. These are pinpoint hemorrhages: petechiae.
Petechiae
Correct. The leg is scattered with small, pinpoint red spots: petechiae, nonblanching skin hemorrhages. Purpura would be larger lesions.
Ecchymoses
Ecchymoses are larger areas of bruising. These spots are pinpoint: petechiae.
Cullen sign
Cullen sign is periumbilical ecchymosis. These are pinpoint spots on a leg: petechiae.
E.alt: The side of a lower leg scattered with many small red pinpoint spots.

E.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of the following: asthma, atelectasis, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pleural effusion
E.q: In which condition does the trachea shift TOWARD the affected side?
opts: Large pleural effusion
A large pleural effusion shifts the trachea toward the UNAFFECTED side, away from the fluid.
Atelectasis
Correct: atelectasis pulls the trachea toward the same side (ipsilateral deviation); a tension pneumothorax or a large effusion pushes it toward the unaffected side.
Tension pneumothorax
Tension pneumothorax shifts the trachea toward the UNAFFECTED side, the opposite direction to atelectasis.
Lobar pneumonia
In pneumonia the trachea stays midline; consolidation increases fremitus but does not move the trachea.

E.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
E.q: Which pair of conditions characteristically causes SUDDEN-onset dyspnea?
opts: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart failure
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is slowly progressive; left-sided heart failure can be gradual or sudden, so the pair is not the sudden one.
Asthma and hyperventilation
Both are EPISODIC: asthma has symptom-free intervals, and hyperventilation comes in episodes at rest or with distress.
Interstitial lung disease and chronic bronchitis
Both are GRADUAL: interstitial lung disease is gradually progressive, and chronic bronchitis is a chronic cough followed by progressive dyspnea.
Pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism
Correct: pneumothorax is sudden with abrupt unilateral pleuritic pain, and pulmonary embolism is sudden, unexplained dyspnea.

E.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
E.q: A silent gap between inspiration and expiration suggests which breath sound?
opts: Bronchovesicular
Bronchovesicular sounds have inspiration and expiration about equal with intermediate pitch; the gap points to bronchial sounds.
Vesicular
Vesicular sounds are the normal sounds over most of the lung, soft and low-pitched, not marked by a silent gap.
Tracheal
Tracheal sounds are heard over the neck and are very loud; the silent gap is the clue named for bronchial sounds.
Bronchial
Correct: a silent gap between inspiration and expiration suggests bronchial breath sounds, which, heard in unexpected places, mean consolidated or fluid-filled lung.

E.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
E.q: Besides known diagnoses, which family-history element should be asked about?
opts: Previous hemoglobinopathy testing

Correct. The family history covers anemia, hemoglobinopathy, abnormal bleeding, unexplained jaundice, relatives requiring transfusions or splenectomy, and known diagnoses with previous genetic or hemoglobinopathy testing.
Relatives' blood types
Blood type is not on the family history. It asks about known diagnoses and previous genetic or hemoglobinopathy testing, with anemia, bleeding and jaundice in relatives.
Relatives' cholesterol levels
Cholesterol is a cardiovascular question. The hematologic family history asks about previous genetic or hemoglobinopathy testing and relatives' transfusions or splenectomy.
Relatives' eye color
Eye color carries no hematologic information. Ask about previous genetic or hemoglobinopathy testing, anemia, bleeding and unexplained jaundice in relatives.

E.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
E.q: Which valves are open during ventricular systole?
opts: The tricuspid and mitral valves
Those close at the start of systole, which is what generates S1.
None of them
The semilunar valves must be open for blood to leave the ventricles.
The pulmonic and aortic valves
Correct — the right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary arteries and the left into the aorta, while the tricuspid and mitral valves are closed.
All four valves
The atrioventricular valves are closed while the semilunar valves are open.

E.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
E.q: Dyspnea comes in episodes with symptom-free intervals, is often worse at night, and is triggered by cold air and exercise. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is sudden, unexplained dyspnea, not a recurring episodic pattern triggered by cold air and exercise.
Interstitial lung disease
Interstitial lung disease is gradually progressive exertional dyspnea with a dry cough, not episodes separated by normal intervals.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
This disease is slowly progressive exertional dyspnea without symptom-free intervals; episodic dyspnea with clear gaps is asthma.
Asthma
Correct: asthma is episodic with symptom-free intervals, often worse at night, with wheezing, cough and chest tightness and triggers such as allergens, exercise and cold air.

E.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
E.q: What usually causes a systolic click?
opts: Mitral stenosis
That produces an opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble.
Pericarditis
That produces a scratchy friction rub rather than a discrete click.
Mitral valve prolapse
Correct — abnormal systolic ballooning of part of the valve into the left atrium, from leaflet redundancy and elongation of the chordae tendineae.
Aortic valve stenosis
That produces a midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur, and may produce an early ejection sound.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 39

E.io: Define the elements of the medical history that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
E.q: Which symptoms raise the possibility of malabsorption as the cause of an anemia?
opts: Chronic diarrhea, bloating and weight loss
Correct. Chronic diarrhea, bloating and weight loss suggest possible malabsorption, and celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease and gastrointestinal surgery are on the exposure history.
Fever, night sweats and travel
Fever, night sweats and travel prompt questions about infection or malignancy. Malabsorption is suggested by chronic diarrhea, bloating and weight loss.
Flooding and intermenstrual bleeding
Those are menstrual bleeding questions, a blood loss source. Malabsorption shows as chronic diarrhea, bloating and weight loss.
Gum bleeding and easy bruising
Those are bleeding-history questions. Malabsorption is suggested by chronic diarrhea, bloating and weight loss.

E.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
E.q: How can palpating the carotid help with murmur timing?
opts: Systolic murmurs match the carotid upstroke
Correct — a systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2, a diastolic one between S2 and S1, and the carotid gives you an external marker for which is which.
The carotid pulse identifies the murmur's intensity
Intensity is graded on the six-point Levine scale rather than by the carotid.
The carotid pulse indicates the shape of the murmur
Shape is the configuration of intensity over time, judged by listening.
Diastolic murmurs coincide with the carotid upstroke
The carotid upstroke marks systole, so it is the systolic murmurs that coincide with it.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 50

E.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
E.q: In which situation is tactile fremitus DECREASED or absent?
opts: Over the top of a large effusion
Toward the TOP of a large pleural effusion fremitus may be increased, even though it is decreased over the fluid itself.
Unilateral pneumonia
Unilateral pneumonia INCREASES fremitus, because consolidated lung transmits the voice better.
Right upper lobe atelectasis
Atelectasis usually diminishes fremitus, but in RIGHT UPPER LOBE atelectasis it may be increased, so this is the exception, not the rule.
Pneumothorax
Correct: fremitus is decreased or absent with a thick chest wall, an obstructed bronchus, obstructive lung disease, effusion, fibrosis, pneumothorax or an infiltrating tumor.

E.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
E.q: Which test has the patient say "ninety-nine" aloud, and is positive when the sound comes through louder?
opts: Egophony
Egophony uses the spoken "ee", which is positive when it sounds like "a".
Whispered pectoriloquy
Whispered pectoriloquy has the patient WHISPER "ninety-nine" or "one-two-three" and is positive when the whisper is louder and clearer.
Diaphragmatic excursion
Diaphragmatic excursion is measured by percussing the level of dullness at expiration and inspiration, not by voice sounds.
Bronchophony
Correct: in bronchophony the patient says "ninety-nine"; muffled and indistinct is normal, louder is positive.

E.io: Identify the physical characteristics of cardiac thrills and murmurs
E.q: What does a pericardial friction rub sound like, and when is it heard?
opts: A harsh crescendo-decrescendo in mid systole
That describes aortic or pulmonic stenosis.
A low-pitched rumble confined to diastole
That describes mitral or tricuspid stenosis.
A blowing decrescendo in early diastole
That describes aortic regurgitation.
Scratchy and scraping, through both phases
Correct — high pitched, best with the diaphragm, plateau shape, most often at Erb's point, and it may increase when the patient leans forward, exhales and holds their breath.
E.cite: PD II Advanced Cardiovascular & Peripheral Vascular System - Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 81

E.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
E.q: Below which hematocrit is a man considered anemic?
opts: 30 percent
30 percent is below both sexes' thresholds; a man at 35 percent is already anemic. The male hematocrit threshold is 40 percent.
35 percent
35 percent is the FEMALE hematocrit threshold. Men are held to a higher one: a hematocrit below 40 percent (or hemoglobin below 13.6 g/dL).
40 percent
Correct. In males anemia is a hemoglobin below 13.6 g/dL (136 g/L) or a hematocrit below 40 percent. Females have the lower thresholds, 11.9 g/dL and 35 percent.
45 percent
45 percent sits above the cut-off and would not define anemia. A man is anemic with a hematocrit below 40 percent.

E.io: Review the anatomical landmarks for a pulmonary physical examination
E.q: Why are needles and tubes placed just over the superior margin of a rib?
opts: The parietal pleura is absent just below each rib
The parietal pleura lines the whole inner rib cage and the upper diaphragm; the rule exists to avoid the neurovascular structures under each rib.
Neurovascular structures run along each rib's upper edge
That reverses it: the neurovascular structures run along the INFERIOR margin, which is why entry is at the superior margin of the rib below.
Neurovascular structures run along each rib's lower edge
Correct: the neurovascular structures run along the inferior margin of each rib, so going in just above the rib below avoids them.
The costal cartilage blocks access below each rib
Costal cartilage is not the reason; the superior-margin rule exists because the neurovascular bundle runs along each rib's lower edge.

E.io: Demonstrate proper clinical skills for a complete and focused pulmonary physical examination
E.q: Crackling felt over the chest wall on palpation, with or without pain, is caused by what?
opts: Small airways snapping open
Airways snapping open produce crackles heard with the stethoscope; crepitus is felt and comes from subcutaneous air.
Consolidated lung beneath
Consolidation increases tactile fremitus; the crackling of crepitus comes from air in the subcutaneous tissue.
Fluid in the pleural space
Pleural fluid dulls percussion and decreases fremitus; it is not what crackles under the skin on palpation.
Air in the subcutaneous tissue
Correct: crepitus is a crackling or grinding over bones, joints or skin due to air in the subcutaneous tissue; with chest wall edema it is seen in mediastinitis.

E.io: Define the elements and physical examination findings that aid in identifying disorders of the hematological system.
E.q: What is koilonychia?
opts: Fine lengthwise ridges in the nail
Longitudinal ridging is a nonspecific nail change. Koilonychia is thin, concave and spoon-shaped.
Thin, concave, spoon-shaped nails
Correct. Koilonychia is thin, concave, spoon-shaped nails, associated with iron deficiency. Like other nail findings it is a supporting clue only.
Bulbous fingertips with a lost nail angle
That is digital clubbing, judged by Schamroth's window and the nail-fold angle, and atypical for uncomplicated anemia. Koilonychia is a spoon-shaped nail.
Pinpoint hemorrhages under the nail
Pinpoint, nonblanching hemorrhages are petechiae, a skin finding. Koilonychia is the spoon-shaped nail.

E.io: Characterize the signs and symptoms of anemia with regard to severity of anemia and specificity.
E.q: Below which hemoglobin is a woman considered anemic?
opts: 10.0 g/dL is well under the cut-off; a woman at 11 g/dL is already anemic. The female threshold is a hemoglobin below 11.9 g/dL or a hematocrit below 35 percent.
Correct. In females anemia is a hemoglobin below 11.9 g/dL (119 g/L) or a hematocrit below 35 percent. The male cut-off is higher, 13.6 g/dL.
13.6 g/dL is the MALE threshold (hematocrit below 40 percent). For females the hemoglobin threshold is lower, below 11.9 g/dL.
15.0 g/dL is above both thresholds and would be normal. Females are anemic below 11.9 g/dL, males below 13.6 g/dL.

E.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings related to abnormal peripheral arterial and venous function
E.q: What may absent peripheral pulses suggest?
opts: Chronic venous insufficiency
Pulses are described as NORMAL in chronic venous insufficiency.
Deep vein thrombosis
Deep vein thrombosis is a venous problem; the arterial pulse is not the finding it produces.
Arterial disorder from atherosclerosis
Correct, with small vessel disease such as diabetes mellitus also to consider. Pulses may also simply be difficult to palpate in obese or muscular patients. Or from systemic embolism.
Pitting edema of any cause
Edema obscures landmarks but is not itself a cause of absent pulses.

E.io: Compare and contrast the physical examination findings of sudden-onset shortness of breath with those of gradual or intermittent presentations
E.q: Episodes of air hunger, sighing, lightheadedness and tingling around the mouth occur at rest during emotional distress. What should be done before attributing them to anxiety?
opts: Consider medical causes first
Correct: this is hyperventilation, and although anxiety may contribute, medical causes must be considered first.
Start an anti-anxiety medication
Treating for anxiety assumes the diagnosis; anxiety may contribute to hyperventilation, but medical causes must be considered first.
Reassure that it is only stress
Reassurance already treats the episodes as anxiety; although anxiety may contribute, medical causes of hyperventilation must be considered first.
Refer for psychiatric evaluation
A psychiatric referral assumes the anxiety diagnosis; medical causes of hyperventilation have to be considered before anxiety is blamed.

E.io: Compare and contrast the cardiac cycle with reference to timing of heart sounds and gallops
E.q: When in the cycle does a click occur, and what follows it?
opts: Early diastole, followed by a rumble
An early diastolic sound followed by a rumble describes an opening snap with mitral stenosis.
Mid to late systole, then a murmur
Correct — the murmur of mitral regurgitation, crescendoing up to S2. The click is high pitched and best heard with the diaphragm at or medial to the apex. The murmur is late systolic.
Just before S1, with no murmur following
A sound occurring just before S1 is S4, the atrial gallop, with the cadence Ten-nes-SEE.
Immediately after S1, with no murmur
A sound shortly after S1 is an early systolic ejection sound.
